collections.title: Europe's Ancient Oaks You Can Actually Visit
collections.intro: An oak does most of its living quietly, which is why so few of the truly old ones get noticed until someone measures the trunk. These eight, pedunculate and holm, span from a Tegel Forest giant that predates Berlin's first written mention to a Barcelona courtyard tree that neighbours spent three years fighting a developer to keep. None survived by being tended like museum pieces. One outlasted a Bavarian duchy. Another grew wider than its older neighbour simply by being left alone. What earns a place here is not age alone: a name, a fight, a naturalist's television campaign, a fence built to protect roots from foot traffic. Every entry is publicly accessible, every coordinate verified, and every page links onward with a map. Start with Berlin's oldest living thing, older than the city itself.

collections.title: Europe's Best Tree City Trips
collections.intro: This list ranks the best afternoon, not the single best tree: cities where several ancient trees stand close enough for one honest walk rather than a taxi between highlights. Every distance and time below comes from the same walk planner every city page already uses, real streets allowed for, not straight lines, and it is a flat-ground number: a hillside city can cost more effort than the kilometres alone suggest, noted plainly where that applies. Order runs easiest first. Lisbon and Sintra are presented as one paired trip, a short train ride apart, so eleven cities carry ten rankings. Every fact here is drawn from this project's own verified research, nothing polled or scored by an algorithm.

collections.title: Europe's 10 Most Remarkable Ancient Trees
collections.intro: This is an opinionated list, and it says so up front. Europe holds tens of thousands of ancient trees; these ten are the most remarkable among the cities we have mapped and verified so far, and the list will shift as new cities join the map. What earns a place here is not age alone. A tree makes this list when it carries a story you can stand next to: a planting date from 1601 with the planter's name attached, a genus named after a family, a churchyard yew that predates the city around it. Every tree is publicly accessible, every location is verified, and every entry links to a full page with map and directions. Start in a London suburb, with the oldest living thing in the city.

collections.title: Europe's Most Remarkable Yews
collections.intro: A yew does not announce its age the way a wide-crowned oak does: the trunk hollows out from the inside, so the tree that looks modest from across a churchyard can be the oldest living thing for miles. These eight, across seven cities, range from a London yew that predates the Roman founding of the city to a Madrid specimen still under two centuries old but split into three fused trunks wide enough to need three separate girth measurements. Several stand guard at entrances, doorways and castle gates, a role yews have played in European gardens for centuries longer than most of the buildings beside them. Every entry is publicly accessible, every coordinate verified. Start with the oldest living thing in London, already ancient when the Romans arrived.

collections.title: Europe's Oldest City Trees Are Mostly Immigrants
collections.intro: Count the ancient trees on this map that stand in European cities and four in ten of them are not European. That is 271 trees out of 686, across 70 of the 79 cities, and the commonest species of the lot is a tree that exists nowhere in the wild: the London plane, a chance hybrid of an American and an Asian parent, which we map 62 times in 35 cities. The rest arrived the way anything else did, by ship and on purpose. A Mexican cypress came with Carmelite missionaries. A black locust arrived as seed posted from the Appalachians. A Californian sequoia was planted in a Paris quarry by an emperor with something to prove. These twelve are the arrivals worth the walk, oldest first.

collections.title: The Ginkgos Worth a November Trip
collections.intro: Ginkgo biloba is the oldest tree lineage on this site by tens of millions of years, a species that outlived the dinosaurs it grew alongside and, in a few documented cases near Hiroshima, outlived a nuclear blast. It also does something almost no other tree manages: every leaf turns the same uniform gold within days of its neighbours, then drops nearly all at once, rather than fading gradually like the rest of autumn. That trick is reason enough to plan a trip around, and these ten specimens, from a 750 year old survivor of the 1945 Tokyo firebombing to a pair planted the same year Milan's botanical garden opened, all perform it within weeks of each other. Most peak in November. Start with the oldest, in a Tokyo temple where a monk's walking staff is said to have taken root eight centuries ago.

collections.title: The Great Planes of Europe
collections.intro: A plane tree does not need to be the oldest thing in a city to be the most memorable. These ten, one per city, got their reputations from a bench eaten alive, a botanist's afternoon walks with Mozart, a bridge widening that moved two full-grown trunks by raft rather than fell them. None are ornamental additions to a park; each is the reason people know that particular corner at all. Start in Dublin, where a Victorian bench has been losing a very slow fight for decades.

collections.title: The Oldest Tree in Every Country We Map
collections.intro: Fifteen countries, one tree each: the oldest verified specimen this site has found in every country it currently maps. Some claims are as solid as a tree gets, an oak whose ring count nearly matches a city's own founding record. Others are genuinely disputed, and say so rather than rounding up. What they share is a place you can actually walk to and stand in front of. Start with the most contested of them all, an Athens olive whose age depends entirely on who you ask.

collections.title: The Oldest Trees We Have Mapped
collections.intro: Four hundred years is a useful threshold. Older than that and a tree predates nearly everything around it: the streets, the houses, usually the city's entire modern shape. This page ranks every tree we have mapped that clears it, oldest first, and it re-ranks itself the moment we add an older one. One rule keeps it honest, and it costs us entries: a tree qualifies on the LOW end of its estimate, so a tree recorded as one hundred to five hundred years old is not here, however tempting the upper number looks. Where the age is a range, the range is what you see, because that is what the sources say. Start at the top with olives that were already ancient when Rome was a village, and work down to oaks that were merely standing when the printing press arrived.

collections.title: Trees Planted by Kings and Their Gardeners
collections.intro: A monarch's word could put a tree in the ground and keep it there for centuries, and enough of them did that the result reads like an itinerary of vanished courts. A retired Japanese emperor carried his own camphor north in 1160 to plant it at a shrine he had just founded. A shogun kept his pine as a bonsai in a pot and only let it touch soil after his death. Henri IV's own herbalist raised Paris's oldest tree from an American seed, and his son planted the second inside the king's own medicinal garden. Queen Victoria planted a Californian sequoia on Irish soil in 1861 and started a habit every visiting head of state since has copied. None of these merely grow in a royal park. Someone with a crown, or a court appointment, specifically wanted each one exactly there.

collections.title: Trees That Outlived Their City
collections.intro: A tree does not know it is a monument until the buildings around it stop being ones. These six watched a temple burn to the ground, a palace flatten in an air raid, a revolution take the man who planted them, and kept growing anyway, the one part of the view that did not need rebuilding afterward. None of them survived by being protected: most were simply too far from the blast, the flame front, or the guillotine to matter to whoever was doing the destroying. What they share now is a strange kind of authority: ask one of these trees what a lost building looked like, and it is the only witness left standing. Start with a Tokyo ginkgo that took a direct hit and kept its scorch marks to prove it.

collections.title: Trees With a Known Planting Date
collections.intro: Almost every ancient tree on this site carries an estimate: a ring count, a girth measurement fed into a growth curve, a guess dressed up as a fact. These fourteen do not. Somewhere in a garden's own ledger, a shrine's dated tradition or a city's own peace festival records, someone wrote down the year a sapling went into the ground, and the record survived along with the tree. The span runs from a Medici garden in Florence, where the botanist who planted the yew in 1720 kept the books himself, to an Antwerp linden planted on a single named day in 1994. Between them: a plane tree that watched Napoleon abdicate, an oak planted for one dead soldier and all his comrades, and a fig gardeners put in the ground by mistake. Age by inference is common here. Age by paperwork is rare, and it changes what a visit means.

collections.title: Wisteria and Blossom Worth a Spring Trip
collections.intro: Spring is the one season no evergreen can compete with. These eleven trees, across nine cities, each have a real, documented peak between late February and the end of May: an orange grove that scents an entire cathedral courtyard, a wisteria a 19th century woodblock master painted from life, chestnut avenues that turn whole boulevards white with flower. None of these moments are guessed. Every one is sourced to the tree's own species and climate, not applied as decoration. Start in Seville, where the blossom comes earliest.

parks.name: the Arnold Arboretum
parks.intro: Harvard's Arnold Arboretum has been formally cataloguing every plant on its grounds since 1872, so its oldest trees come with a paper trail most cities can only guess at. A white oak on Peters Hill was already growing wild when the Arboretum absorbed the land, and it took until 2010 for anyone to accession it into the record and 2018 to core-sample it to a germination date in the early 1800s. A Franklin tree in the Explorers Garden descends from a species that has not grown wild anywhere on earth for roughly two hundred years, ever since John Bartram found it on a few acres of Georgia riverbank in 1765 and the wild population vanished within a generation. A dawn redwood by the Hunnewell Visitor Center grew from a 1948 seed shipment out of Hubei, China, sent after the species turned up alive in the Chinese interior having previously been known only from fossils. A paperbark maple in the Maple Collection is one of two seedlings a single plant collector dug out of a Chinese wood in 1907, the shared ancestor of nearly every paperbark maple now growing in America. And two katsura trees along Meadow Road began as seed mailed from Sapporo in 1878 by the college president who helped found what is now Hokkaido University. All are open to the public, free, every day of the year.

parks.name: Castle Park
parks.intro:
Kasteel Helmond has stood in the middle of this town for nearly seven hundred years, a moated brick castle that is now the town hall and museum. Until the middle of the twentieth century it sat inside a much larger landscape park; the 1921 sale of the estate began the park's disappearance, and these seven trees are what survived it.

The oldest is a pedunculate oak, planted between 1880 and 1890 while the castle was still a private house, four decades before that sale. Its neighbour is stranger than it looks: the national register files it as a European beech, but its own description says otherwise, that it is a Chinese beech, Fagus engleriana, grafted onto ordinary rootstock because the species will not seed itself in Dutch soil, and as far as anyone knows the oldest and thickest of its kind in the country.

The rest of the grounds fill in around them. A silver maple and a silver lime span the decades either side of the 1921 sale. Two horse chestnuts stand about fifty metres apart, planted a decade apart, for the conkers as much as anything. And a common holly, an odd formality for a shrub, grows exactly where the register itself says it cannot be seen from any path, the one tree here you will have to go looking for.

All seven stand on open castle grounds in the centre of Helmond, free to walk to any day of the year.

parks.name: Central Park
parks.intro:
Central Park's oldest tree is probably the black tupelo in the Ramble, at about 168 years. Probably, because a multi-trunked London plane near the Reservoir may date to 1862, when the Reservoir itself was dug, and neither tree comes with proof: the tupelo has the better paperwork, the plane has more trunks than any ageing rule of thumb can handle, and they disagree by only four years.

That the contest is this close says something about the ground. The park opened in 1858 on swamp, rock and scattered farms with no old trees at all, so everything standing today was planted, and its oldest survivors are a record of what the park's own gardeners chose rather than what nature left behind.

Two of the seven trees here are American elms from the Mall's Literary Walk, one of the last major stands of the species anywhere after Dutch elm disease took most of the country's street elms from the 1930s on. A third elm, gnarled and wide-canopied at the East 97th Street entrance, is old enough that nobody wrote down its planting year. Between them stand a small grove of Lebanon cedars planted for a family's grandchildren, and 35 Yoshino cherries whose planting predates the more famous gift Washington received the same year, 1912. All free, every day, dawn to dusk.

parks.name: the City Botanic Gardens
parks.intro: Queensland's oldest public garden opened in 1855, and Walter Hill, its first curator, spent the next three decades filling it with plants brought in from across the world; the results are still standing. Seven of the trees we map grow here: the tree that started Australia's whole macadamia industry, a banyan with the finest aerial-root structure of its species in the country, the tallest tree in the gardens at forty-five metres, and a fig said to descend from the tree the Buddha sat under. All are free to walk past, a few minutes apart on paths in the middle of Brisbane's CBD.

parks.name: Fort Canning Park
parks.intro: Fort Canning Hill was the seat of the ancient Kingdom of Singapura before it was a British fort or a public park, and the five heritage trees mapped on it now sit on ground that has been fought over, planted over and walked over for seven centuries. A rain tree spreads its canopy directly above the public stairway that carries walkers out onto Hill Street, so most people pass beneath it without looking up. A Madras thorn beside the Service Reservoir is the largest of its species on Singapore's whole heritage register, its girth measured twice, eleven years apart, and grown wider both times. A tamalan on Fort Green is one of the last survivors of an ornamental planting scheme laid out across the hill in the early 1900s, when the old fort grounds became a colonial pleasure garden; NParks' own register notes that few of its neighbours from that planting are still alive. A terap nasi grows beside the hill's 14th Century Walk of History with plank buttresses broad enough to make its age feel physical rather than just recorded. And an earpod tree, named in both English and Spanish for seed pods coiled like a human ear, stands between the old fort wall and the hotel that now shares the hill with it. All five are NParks-registered heritage trees, free to see, on park ground open around the clock.

parks.name: Fota Arboretum
parks.intro: Fota Island sits at the same latitude as Newfoundland, and the only reason its arboretum can grow a Canary Island date palm and a camphor tree from southern China outdoors is the Gulf Stream, which keeps this stretch of Cork Harbour close to frost-free. The Smith-Barry family began building the collection here in the 1820s on what had been ordinary farmland, and the national heritage tree survey's oldest find, a holm oak banded to 200 to 300 years, predates that start and would have already been standing when they began. The rest of the collection is younger and stranger: a Campbell's magnolia that covers itself in dinner-plate pink flowers for about ten days each late winter before it leafs at all; a Japanese cedar cultivar whose every needle grows in a tight curl, a Victorian nursery mutation nicknamed Granny's Ringlets; a New Zealand conifer with no true leaves, its flattened stem tissue notched enough to look like celery; and a coast redwood that in its native California would be the tallest tree species on Earth, here still a child of 150 to 200 years next to the two-thousand-year specimens back home. Free to visit, on the same island as Fota Wildlife Park.

parks.name: the Giardini Montanelli
parks.intro: Milan's first public park, laid out in 1784, and the trees in it have been measured more carefully than almost anywhere else in the city. Six of them are on the monumental register. The largest plane in Milan grows here, spreading sideways rather than up; a bald cypress that gardeners called a metasequoia for years until somebody checked the genus properly; and the widest of Milan's three Caucasian wingnuts, five and a half metres round. One plane has become a research subject in its own right, with the city counting what lives on it.

parks.name: the Giardino dei Semplici
parks.intro: Cosimo I de' Medici founded this garden in 1545 to grow medicinal plants, which makes it the third oldest botanical garden in the world and older than most of what surrounds it. The name means the garden of the simples, simples being the single-ingredient herbs a physician worked from before pharmacy existed. Seven of the trees we map grow inside its walls, and several are the kind of specimen a botanical garden accumulates precisely because somebody was paid to keep them alive for four hundred years.

parks.name: the Giardino Inglese
parks.intro: Maria Carolina of Austria wanted an English garden and got one of the first in Italy, which is why the trees here are strange. She commissioned it in 1786 at the top of the Reggia's enormous formal park, and the English gardener John Andrew Graefer filled it with species the country had barely seen: a camphor tree from Japan, a cork oak, a Douglas fir from the American northwest, a sweet osmanthus. Seven of them are on the register today. The oldest is a yew by the Bath of Venus that was carried in fully grown, which makes it older than the garden it stands in.

parks.name: Hortus Botanicus Amsterdam
parks.intro: The Hortus Botanicus Amsterdam has been growing rare plants on the same corner of the Plantage since 1638, and five of its oldest trees now form a proper collector's walk inside the garden gate. A Turkish hazel planted in 1795, the country's oldest and thickest according to the Dutch tree foundation, flowers with pollen-shedding catkins every January while the rest of the garden sits bare. A few paths over, a shellbark hickory sourced from the wet river bottoms of the American Midwest and a southern catalpa whose trunk corkscrews as it climbs sit close enough to visit in the same stroll, followed by a Turner's oak that keeps its leathery leaves through the whole Dutch winter and a ginkgo, the last living branch of an entire plant order older than the dinosaurs. All five stand a few minutes' walk apart, on the one Hortus ticket.

parks.name: the Hortus Botanicus
parks.intro: Leiden's Hortus Botanicus was founded in 1590, and ten of the city's remarkable trees stand inside it. The tulip tree by professor Herman Boerhaave's name came from a Virginia seed a London apothecary posted across the Channel in October 1716, eleven days before it reached Leiden's soil. The zelkovas came further: Philipp Franz von Siebold, a physician stationed on the Dutch trading post at Deshima in the 1820s, sent home more Japanese plants than any European before him, and the Hortus holds the first zelkovas that ever left the country. A ginkgo planted in 1785 spent a century and a half producing nothing but the small catkins of a male tree, until gardeners grafted female branches onto it in 1935 so it would finally bear seed. A date-plum, which children call the Halloween tree, has holes in its trunk left by a maple that seeded itself inside the older tree's wood in the late 19th century. A horse chestnut at the garden's edge is the thickest of its kind recorded anywhere in the Netherlands, 5.8 metres round by the national monumental tree register's own measurement, its roots reaching almost to the water of the Witte Singel. And a catalpa leaning toward the canal is kept from going in by cables tied to another tree on this same list. The garden is open to the public with an admission charge.

parks.name: the Jardi Botanic
parks.intro: Valencia's university botanic garden moved to this walled plot off Carrer Quart in 1802, and eight of the city's monumental trees now stand inside it, more than any other single place in Valencia. The Kashmir cypress is Bhutan's national tree, kept alive around Buddhist temples for centuries before Western botany even named it. The Caucasian elm grows nothing like an elm, its trunk breaking early into a sheaf of near-vertical branches that reads more like a bundle than a canopy. A Turkish pine went straight up for thirty metres without leaning or forking once, while a silk floss tree, a southern live oak, a Hartwiss oak, a London plane and a river she-oak fill out a collection assembled from four continents. Most of these carry no recorded planting date: the garden's own register measures trunks and crowns but keeps no year, so age here is mostly an open question left for whoever can read a ring count. The garden charges a small admission fee and is open to the public.

parks.name: Leijpark
parks.intro:
Leijpark's oldest trees were planted by men who needed the wages. Leonard Springer, the most sought-after garden architect in the Netherlands, drew the 30-hectare park in 1919, his last large design, and then nothing happened for fifteen years while the land was assembled. It was finally built between 1934 and 1939 as a work relief project in the depths of the Depression, in the English landscape manner along the little river Leij that gives it its name. A silver maple, the first tree in the park to do anything after winter, and a young pedunculate oak that will outlast every other tree here by centuries both went in with that original planting.

Tucked in the park's far northeast corner, in ground still locally called the Kloosterparkbos, stand three older trees the wider design absorbed rather than planted: an oak, a lime and a large-leaved holly, all named for a convent, home to the Congregatie van Onze Lieve Vrouw der Afzondering in het Cenakel from 1908, whose garden this land used to be before it was redeveloped and folded into Springer's park. The convent is gone; the trio it left behind, roughly 120 years old, makes an easy five-minute extension to the walk. All of it is free, open daily, no ticket.

parks.name: Nara Park
parks.intro:
The oldest dated tree in Nara Park is a black pine at the corner of the block that holds Kofuku-ji's National Treasure Hall, about two hundred and fifty years old and three and a half metres round. Gardeners of the Edo period planted black pines through the park for no reason except that they looked right, and this one outgrew all the others. Flying squirrels still work its cone crop at night, stripping the seeds and leaving the cores scattered on the path beneath it in a shape locals compare to fried prawns.

Two more trees carry no recorded age but stand on ground that dates them anyway. A soapberry beside the approach to Kasuga Taisha has a bamboo growing up through its hollow trunk and out of the crown, so what looks like one tree is actually two, a plant nurses have described as a mother holding a child. Its black seeds strung prayer beads and filled the shuttlecocks of the New Year game hanetsuki. A chinaberry stands where Todai-ji's seven-storey east pagoda once rose above the park before it burned for the last time, planted, by tradition, because the species was believed to keep evil from ground where the dead were remembered.

The youngest tree here is also the one people mistake for a single giant: three camphors planted in 1908 on the spot where Emperor Meiji watched army manoeuvres have grown together into one unbroken dome, nearly five metres round at the thickest trunk and reaching twenty-six metres up. The park's deer graze right to the fence around them. A fifth tree, broad-canopied and mature beside a pond and a wooden rest pavilion somewhere between Todai-ji and Kasuga Taisha, arrived as a reader's photograph rather than a known record, and neither its species nor its exact pond has been settled yet. If you know the spot, tell us; that is how the fifth tree gets its name.

parks.name: the National Botanic Gardens
parks.intro: The Dublin Society founded the National Botanic Gardens at Glasnevin in 1795 to teach scientific agriculture, and the collecting habit that started then never stopped. A 2009 heritage survey by the Tree Council of Ireland recorded six of these seven trees as Exceptional Specimen Trees, gathered from three continents across two centuries of curators, all within 200 metres of each other: a dawn redwood grown from the seed that ended the species' presumed extinction in China, an Atlas cedar from a mountain range now losing its wild population to drought, a Caucasian elm so admired a County Offaly nurseryman propagated cuttings from it and sold the result as its own named cultivar, and a bald cypress built for Louisiana swampland doing its best in an Irish flower bed. The seventh and oldest, a formal double avenue of yew, carries the garden's separate Named Trees designation and is said, by tradition rather than record, to have been planted in memory of the essayist Joseph Addison before the gardens themselves existed. Entry is free, every day except Christmas Day, and all seven specimens sit an easy afternoon's walk from each other.

parks.name: Orto Botanico di Lucca
parks.intro: Lucca's botanical garden was founded in 1820 by Maria Luisa di Borbone, Duchess of Lucca, and its early directors recorded exact planting dates for several of these trees. A cedar of Lebanon and a Corsican pine went in together in 1822; a redwood arrived around 1850, one of the first raised in Europe; a ginkgo, felled by lightning, regrew as three trunks from one root. By the pond, a pair of bald cypresses throw up woody knees from the water and turn rust orange each autumn, the garden's only conifer that behaves like a deciduous tree. Nearby, a seven-metre Balearic box grows to a size the species rarely reaches outside its native islands, next to the garden's youngest registered tree, a silver lime planted around 1900, and a fastigiate yew whose thickness belies how slowly the species grows. The garden charges standard admission.

parks.name: the Orto Botanico di Padova
parks.intro: The University of Padua founded this garden in 1545 to teach medical students which plants their patients were actually being given, the first botanical garden anywhere attached to a university and the model every later one copied. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1997, citing its continuous four-and-a-half centuries of scientific use rather than its age alone. Five of the trees we map grow inside its circular walls, among them a dwarf palm Goethe wrote about, a ginkgo grafted to bear both pollen and fruit from one trunk, and Italy's first Himalayan cedar. Admission is a paid ticket, and worth it.

parks.name: the Real Orto Botanico
parks.intro: Founded by Napoleonic decree in 1807 and planted with things Naples had never seen, which is why four of these five trees come from other continents. The widest trunk on Naples' entire national register stands here, a silk floss tree whose bulging green trunk looks less like timber than like something inflated. Beside it grows a Chilean wine palm, a species nearly drunk out of existence because its trunk is full of sweet sap that was tapped for wine. The exception is the ginkgo, which is not a novelty from far away but a survivor from far back.

parks.name: the Parc de la Ciutadella
parks.intro: This park is a fortress the city pulled down. The citadel that gave it its name was built to hold Barcelona after 1714, demolished in the 1870s, and the ground rebuilt as the city's first public park for the Universal Exposition of 1888, which is why almost everything old here dates from one fifteen year window. A Mexican white oak went in around 1887 and is the only one of its kind alive in Catalonia. A river she-oak followed beside the Cascada around 1894, its drooping grey green needles actually jointed twigs. A silk tree has flowered every July since about 1896, well past the age its species normally reaches. The stoutest black locust in Barcelona is here, 4.3 metres around on twelve metres of tree, and so is a plane nobody has ever cut back to knuckles, which is simply what the species does when left alone.

parks.name: the Parc d'Egmont
parks.intro: Brussels started its official inventory of remarkable trees in this park, with a squat evergreen oak that most people walk past. The Parc d'Egmont is small, hidden behind the shops of the Avenue Louise, and holds six of the trees we map within a couple of minutes of each other, which makes it one of the densest pockets on the site. Among them is a ginkgo that is the seventh thickest recorded anywhere in the region and is being slowly damaged by the people who like it, and a tulip tree formally adopted by an art institute a few streets away.

parks.name: the Parco del Valentino
parks.intro: Turin's oldest tree and Turin's tallest tree both stand in this park, a few hundred metres apart along the Po. The oldest is an oak behind the Castello del Valentino, past two hundred years by the regional register and the exception in a city where every other tree that old is a plane. The tallest is a plane by the Fontana dei Dodici Mesi at forty metres, and nothing in Turin beats it. A third plane, six metres round, is the widest trunk in the park, and a hackberry stands alone on open grass, which is why its crown is so even.

parks.name: Park Sonsbeek
parks.intro:
Park Sonsbeek's oldest claim stands beside a monument to a man who never saw it planted: a pedunculate oak dated to somewhere between 1750 and 1800, growing next to the 1931 memorial to physicist Hendrik Lorentz. The national register that puts an age on it is more taken with the shape than the years.

Four more pedunculate oaks share the park with it, and no two came by their trouble the same way. Two stand together at the edge of the Sonsbeek meadow, thick and tall enough that the register flags both for condition rather than just girth. A third grows alone in a grazed field where the corner meets Sonsbeekweg, and the electric fencing kept up for the livestock has also kept surveyors from getting a tape around it properly for years. A fourth, by the old Witte Watermolen, carries no name and no plaque, only a regular stop on the park ranger's own guided walk each Open Monument Day.

The other two trees break the pattern. A yew planted around 1850 has grown a waist over three metres round, genuinely rare for the species in the Netherlands. A copper beech, its purple leaves a colour mutation gardeners have propagated for centuries rather than a species of its own, was planted between the Sonsbeek villa and its pond sometime in the 1830s. All six stand on open parkland, free to walk to any day of the year.

parks.name: the Parque del Retiro
parks.intro: The Retiro was a royal private garden for two hundred years before Madrid was let in, and that is why its trees are old. Philip IV's court laid it out in the 1630s as the grounds of a palace that has since vanished, leaving the planting behind; the park only became public in 1868. Nine of the trees we map stand inside it, and they are spread wide enough that finding them is a proper afternoon rather than a lap of the pond. The oldest is a Montezuma cypress near the Paseo de Mexico, a species from central Mexico that arrived in Spain with the empire and outlived it.

parks.name: the Prinsentuin
parks.intro: Leeuwarden's Prinsentuin was laid out between 1822 and 1824 on the site of the city's former fortifications, making it close to the oldest public park in the Netherlands, and five of its oldest trees are old enough to remember that opening. Its horse chestnut, banded by the national monumental tree register to 1820 and 1830, is almost exactly as old as the park itself. A European beech stands by the Pier Pander Temple, a small classical building put up in 1924 to hold the work of the Frisian sculptor born in 1864 to a rag merchant's family and remembered here for the talent that got him out of it. A second beech grows behind Tresoar, the Frisian historical and literary archive, keeping company with a language that has spent centuries arguing over its own literature. An ash by the park's tea house carries a crown the register itself calls one-sided, the shape a tree gets when the trees standing next to it crowd out the light on one side and not the other. And a Canadian poplar nearby has a trunk so deeply grooved and studded with fist and head sized burrs that it reads more like rock than wood. All five stand in a park that has never charged admission.

parks.name: the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens
parks.intro: Five of the six trees mapped here came from somewhere else, and the sixth is Australian without being Tasmanian. A Douglas fir out of the Pacific Northwest went into the ground in 1894, seven years before the Australian colonies federated, and measured 30 metres when the National Trust looked at it in 2014. Two giant sequoias planted together in 1879 still mark the entrance drive. A Queensland kauri, a rainforest tree from the warm wet coast far to the north, reaches 39 metres here at 42 degrees south and is listed on Hobart's register under four headings at once, where most trees carry one. A chir pine from the dry Himalayan foothills droops needles thirty centimetres long. The spotted gum is the local one, and even it grows wild in New South Wales rather than on this island.

parks.name: the Schlosspark Nymphenburg
parks.intro: Munich protects trees by law here for reasons written down in a city ordinance, and two of these five are protected for being odd rather than big. A large-leaved lime by the Badenburger See is listed as bizarrer und knorriger Wuchs, bizarre and gnarled growth, which is an unusually honest thing for a legal document to say. There is also a weeping beech protected partly because people are fond of it, an oak in the Dorfchen, the part of a royal garden built to look undesigned, and a fern-leaved beech of a form that did not exist anywhere before about 1804.

parks.name: Singapore Botanic Gardens
parks.intro: Singapore's Botanic Gardens opened in 1859 and earned a UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2015, not for any single specimen but for grounds that have kept unusually good paperwork on the trees growing in them. A sausage tree arrived from Honolulu on 13 May 1931 and went into the ground that October, one of dozens of tropical trials from an era when a plant's usefulness decided its future. A cannon ball tree grew from a seed the assistant director E.J.H. Corner grabbed during a rushed eight-hour stop at the botanic garden in Peradeniya, Ceylon, the same year. A baobab, moved once in 1996 and only about forty years old, already carries five metres of girth, a fraction of the age a species that can pass a thousand years usually needs for that. A giant strangler fig by Swan Lake is registered as a Burmese banyan, though a 2024 study argues it is something else entirely, propagated here from cuttings for more than 150 years. A saga tree planted in the 1880s to smother weed grass now sits in the National Heritage Board's own art collection, photographed for a 2013 work mapping the island's saga trees. Two nutmeg trees near the old Economic Garden are what is left of the spice boom that gave Orchard Road its name. All eight stand on garden ground open daily and free to enter.

parks.name: Villa Borghese
parks.intro: Cardinal Scipione Borghese built this park in the early 1600s as a showcase for his art collection, and his gardener planted the trees to match: oriental planes brought in as a novelty, arranged in a valley that still carries their name. Adonis, the oldest of them, has stood here for over four centuries and outlived the villa's original owner by nearly as long. A cedar leans over the lake a few minutes' walk away, and past the boating lake stands what one conservation group calls the last survivor of the eighteen cypresses planted around Piazza di Siena in 1789, the arena that still hosts Rome's international horse show every year. Deeper into the park's holm oak wood, behind the museum that now holds a de Chirico and Warhol collection, a pair of hackberries with a four-metre girth waits on the official monumental status that roughly thirty of the park's other old trees are still queuing for.

parks.name: Vosseparkje
parks.intro: Vosseparkje, officially Westerpark, exists because Leeuwarden needed a reservoir more than it needed a park. Garden architect Gerrit Vlaskamp landscaped the grounds around the city's drinking-water works in 1872, and the park he drew was redesigned once more in 1926, by which point most of its oldest trees were already decades in the ground. Seven of them sit on the Dutch national monument register today, all inside a few minutes' walk of each other. A Caucasian wingnut from the Caspian forests carries a trunk over a metre round and a scar from a 1987 ice storm. A black locust planted in 1924 has spent a century leaning and is now held up by a prop. Two feather elms of the same narrow cultivar stand at opposite ends of the park, told apart by which one is nearer the pond, and an oak by the south-east entrance has stumped the register itself: its own entry reads Caucasian or Persian oak, undecided, and nobody has settled which. Free, open, no ticket.

parks.name: Wilhelminapark
parks.intro: Leonard Springer drew the Wilhelminapark in the 1890s and opened it to the public in May 1898, and part of what makes it worth a visit is that he built around ground that already had trees on it rather than a blank field. Tilburg's oldest elm, on the Dutch national monument register, was standing here before Springer arrived, and a Canadian poplar nearby is older still, from a planting band of 1860 to 1870, decades before the park existed. Springer's own planting survives too: a weeping silver lime he put in himself in 1898, dated to the year in the register's own note, and a flowering ash from the northwest corner that the register admits you can barely see. The fifth tree breaks the pattern entirely. A Pontic oak from the 1970s, a species found wild only in one pocket of northeast Turkey and the Caucasus, is protected not for its age but for what it is, a rarity the register lists under a single word: dendrological. All five stand within a few minutes of each other, free and open daily.

parks.name: the York Museum Gardens
parks.intro: Ten acres of botanical garden laid over the ruins of a wrecked abbey, which is a strange thing to walk through and an excellent thing for trees. The Yorkshire Philosophical Society made these gardens in the 1830s around the remains of St Mary's Abbey, dissolved by Henry VIII three centuries earlier, and planted them as a scientific collection rather than a lawn. Six of the trees we map stand here, all within a few minutes of each other, which makes this the tightest cluster in the city and one of the tightest anywhere on the site.

parks.name: Zuiderpark
parks.intro:
The five oldest trees in Zuiderpark stand on an ordinary residential corner because they used to be a classroom. Between 1953 and 1967, evening students training as horticulturists and florists were examined here, on their feet, on the Latin and Dutch names of the trees around them, along a route locals nicknamed the zweetlaantje, the sweat lane, for how it felt to be quizzed in front of an instructor. The trees they were tested on still ring the site of the municipal nursery that trained them.

A Caucasian wingnut misnamed 'Japanese' in its own register entry. An American yellowwood whose cut wood runs bright yellow. A pecan, a species that belongs to the warm river valleys of the American south, growing in Brabant since the 1950s. A Transcaucasian birch kept in its rare single-trunked tree form rather than the shrub shape the species usually takes. A golden beech that never really turns green at all. None of them are old by this project's usual standard, all roughly seventy years, and each one's only record is a single national register entry with no independent account. Their case for a page rests on what they were planted to do: give a generation of students something unfamiliar to learn. The school moved on in 1967. The trees, and the lesson, are still free to walk past.

countries.name: Australia
countries.intro: Australia's old trees keep two different kinds of time. Melbourne's elms have grown to a size and age Europe lost, because Dutch elm disease never crossed the water; its Osage orange on Yarra Boulevard is dated to the 1860s, among the oldest plantings the site maps here. Hobart's Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, founded in 1818 and the country's second-oldest, holds a Douglas fir older than Australian Federation itself, planted in 1894, alongside dawn redwoods of a species known only from fossils until a living stand was found in China in 1941. Brisbane's City Botanic Gardens, laid out from 1855, grew the tree that started the country's entire macadamia industry, dated from trials beginning 1858. Nothing mapped here is ancient by European or Japanese standards; almost everything is a nineteenth-century planting that got lucky with a climate and a curator who tried something unusual.

countries.name: Austria
countries.intro: Vienna keeps a tree register detailed enough to argue with itself. The oldest plane in front of the City Hall is dated 1783 by tradition and 1876 in the city's own records, ninety years apart with no way from here to settle it. The pagoda tree in the Stadtpark is on file as planted in 1860, in a park that did not open until August 1862. The friction is worth it: the register holds nearly nine hundred trees in the eighth district alone, which is why a girth or a planting year exists here where most cities have neither. Vienna also has one of the strangest trees on this site, a ginkgo at Schönbrunn carrying a grafted female branch, so a single tree is both sexes at once. Sixty trees are mapped so far, across Vienna, Graz, Salzburg, the lakeside cluster of protected yews around Hallstatt, and three single-tree destinations, a yew at Gutau, a mountain maple at Ramsau am Dachstein, and a disputed thousand-year oak at Bad Blumau.

countries.name: Belgium
countries.intro: Belgium keeps a national champion for each species, and one small Antwerp park hemmed in by three streets holds two of them: the thickest black locust recorded in the country at 4.10 metres, and a black mulberry at 1.28 metres, which is what a record looks like for a tree that never grows stout. Brussels runs an inventory of its own, and the first entry in it was a squat evergreen oak in the Parc d'Egmont that most people walk straight past. Six of the trees mapped here stand in that one park, within a couple of minutes of each other. The largest tree in Brussels by girth is not European at all: a giant sequoia in the Parc de Woluwe, measured at 8.66 metres around in 2017. Ten cities so far, 63 trees.

countries.name: Brazil
countries.intro: Brazil's most famous tree by international record is not its oldest. The Cajueiro de Pirangi, a single cashew whose branches root wherever they touch the ground, has spread across roughly 8,500 square metres near Natal and held the Guinness record for the largest cashew tree since 1994, at the modest age of about 138. The genuinely old trees keep quieter company: O Patriarca, a jequitiba-rosa in the cerrado of Vassununga State Park, is called the country's oldest by a press that cannot agree whether that means 600 years or more than 3,000. Rio de Janeiro supplies the range in between, a sumauma linked to Tom Jobim, a fig tree with a disputed two centuries behind it, a baobab that arrived on ships from Africa long before anyone thought to write its age down. Three cities mapped so far, eight trees, from a single record-holding cashew to a rainforest giant nobody can date.

countries.name: Bulgaria
countries.intro: Bulgaria's oldest tree is not its most impressive one to look at anymore. A 1982 core sample counted 1,637 rings in the Granit Oak, dating its germination to around 345 and giving Bulgaria a tree age nobody has to guess at, but a 1969 storm and falling groundwater have since reduced it to a single living branch. Higher up, in Pirin National Park above Bansko, Baikushev's Pine carries a gentler kind of age claim: tradition holds it was already standing when Khan Asparuh founded the First Bulgarian Empire around 681, a repeated figure of about 1,300 years rather than a measured one. Sofia supplies the political history in between, a mulberry linked to national hero Vasil Levski, an oak named for the poet Pencho Slaveykov, a spruce planted for Ivan Vazov. Four cities mapped so far, seven trees, from a dying record-holder to a living tradition.

countries.name: Canada
countries.intro: Canada's mapped trees keep circling one epidemic. Dutch elm disease killed roughly 22,000 of Montreal's American elms, and the Last Elm of Mont-Royal is one of the few left, a self-seeded survivor growing away from the streets where the disease moved fastest. Quebec City's Plains of Abraham lost most of its mature elms the same way and still keeps about 750 of them, monitored tree by tree against the fungus a century on, alongside wych elms, a European species growing beside the American ones. Toronto took a different route: in 2022 the city named an official tree for the first time, a 220-year-old red oak in Kew Gardens with a trunk 5.3 metres round. Montreal also holds a honey locust dated from a death recorded on the gravestone beside it, and a Japanese yew that grew fifteen metres wide instead of tall.

countries.name: China
countries.intro: China's oldest trees cluster around two kinds of ground: imperial temples and religious mountains. Beijing graded its ancient trees by class under the Qing and named ten "ancient tree kings" in 2018, five of which stand here, among them cypresses planted for state altars and a ginkgo that queues photographers every November. Further west, on the Tibetan plateau's edge, Bon tradition holds a giant cypress outside Nyingchi as the life tree of the religion's own founder, at up to 3,200 years the oldest tree this site maps anywhere. A ginkgo at Shaolin Temple carries a monks-training legend in the holes through its trunk, and a banyan on the Jinbao River near Yangshuo was a film location decades before anyone measured its age. Hong Kong's banyans are civic rather than sacred, rooted into a colonial trading port's walls and stairs.

countries.name: Czech Republic
countries.intro: The thickest protected tree in Prague measures seven and a half metres around, and the story everyone tells about it, that Beethoven sat beneath it, is almost certainly false. The city's register says as much rather than repeating it, which sets the tone for the rest. Prague dates its trees in ranges and admits where two records disagree by eighty years, as they do for the ginkgo in Stromovka. Brno keeps its own list: the Bystrc Lime, past 400 years old, survived a 1933 fire when a neighbour tried to smoke a marten out of its hollow trunk by setting it alight. Cesky Krumlov's oldest tree turns the usual pattern round: it is the free one, a village-square lime older than the paid monastery lindens nearby. Beyond the three cities, seventeen single-tree villages carry the country's national Tree of the Year winners and its stranger stories: Teleci's hollow lime a person can stand inside, Rimov's pilgrimage linden that once held 51 people inside its trunk at once, an oak near Lukavice its own estate once tried to kill by stripping the soil from its roots, and a beech at a mountain border crossing that is not the famous tree it replaced. Twenty-one places, 60 trees mapped so far.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.intro: Copenhagen's remarkable trees come with tape measurements, which is rarer than it should be. The Danish dendrological society has surveyed them one by one and filed them under working names: a beech in Frederiksberg Have is registered as Bøgen ved Bådfarten, the beech by the boat trip, which makes it the easiest tree in the city to find. A honey locust has been on record since a gardening magazine featured it in 1941. Assistens cemetery holds five of the sixteen mapped here, and the thickest tree inside its walls is a sycamore, the least exotic species in it. The oldest is Skovfogedegen, a hollow oak 11 km north of the city at the edge of the royal deer park, which three Danish sources date to around the year 1200. The country's most famous oak is not in either city: Kongeegen stands propped and hollow in Jaegerspris Nordskov, the last of three named oaks in that wood, with Storkeegen dead in 1980 and Snoegen in 1991. Two single trees have their own places too: Ambrosius-egen on Tåsinge, redated from 700 to roughly 400 years by a 1997 core sample, and Svalebøgen in Gjerrild, a fused beech failing since a trunk came down in 2022. Twenty-six trees mapped so far, across five places.

countries.name: Finland
countries.intro: This far north, cold winters and thin, rocky soil slow a tree down, so Finland's list runs on rarity more than raw age. Helsinki only became the capital in 1812 and most of its ten protected trees are Finnish size records, a thickest willow, a thickest park lime, rather than genuine veterans. Turku's Kalm's Oak earns its place differently: planted around 1750 in a garden the Great Fire of 1827 burned to the ground around it, and still called the city's oldest tree. Outside both cities stands Paavola's Oak on Lohjansaari, documented by the photographer I.K. Inha over a century ago and repeatedly called the most beautiful tree in the country since long before anyone here was searching the internet for it. Twelve trees mapped so far, across Helsinki, Turku and Lohja.

countries.name: France
countries.intro: France's oldest tree has a birth certificate rather than an estimate. The Robinier of Square Rene-Viviani in Paris was planted in 1601 by Jean Robin, herbalist to Henri IV, from seed the naturalist John Tradescant sent from the Appalachians, before the Mayflower sailed and before the genus that now carries Robin's name even existed. That precision runs through France's other oldest trees, most raised from seed by royal gardeners and university botanists rather than found growing wild: a Cedar of Lebanon that legend says crossed the Channel tucked inside a botanist's hat, a plane tree named for the naturalist Buffon who ran the garden that raised it. Seven cities carry that botanical lineage, Paris alongside Lyon's, Nice's, Bordeaux's, Strasbourg's, Toulouse's and Rouen's own plantings. The rest of the map is single-tree destinations of a different kind: a Norman oak with two working chapels built into its hollow trunk, a Breton oak on the edge of Broceliande, a hollow Calvados yew wide enough to hold thirty people, an oak in Ille-et-Vilaine covered in devotional offerings since 1792, a Weppes lime cited to a 1490 deed that outlasted a chateau and a world war, a solitary Lot-et-Garonne oak that survived a 2022 trunk fissure the year after being named the country's Tree of the Year. French ancient trees tend to come with an actual planting year rather than a growth-ring guess, because someone with a reputation to protect wrote the date down. 34 places mapped so far, 124 trees.

countries.name: Germany
countries.intro: Germany protects individual trees the way other countries protect buildings. A Naturdenkmal is a legal designation attached to one named object, and the reason for it gets written down: Munich's 2021 ordinance protects a lime by the Badenburger See for bizarrer und knorriger Wuchs, bizarre and gnarled growth, and an ash on Leinthalerstrasse for an extremely wide spreading crown, with no age, no measurement and nothing else on file. Nuremberg fits six separately protected trees onto 1.7 hectares of one small park that used to be a quarantine station. Berlin supplies the age: Dicke Marie, in the Tegel Forest, had probably been growing for a long time before the city got its first written mention in 1237. Bamberg supplies the opposite case, four trees with no age recorded for any of them, a pattern that repeats in Stuttgart, Freiburg and Heidelberg, whose registers name and protect a tree without ever measuring it. 64 cities and 200 trees are mapped so far, and the paperwork here is usually better than the dating.

countries.name: Greece
countries.intro: The three Greek places mapped here answer the age question in different ways. Thessaloniki took core samples from four plane trees in 2019: 828 years for the one below the Byzantine walls, then 310, 235 and 205 for the others. Athens works in inheritance: the olive beside the Erechtheion is tied by Herodotus to the Persian sack of 480 BC, though the wood standing today is only 70 to 110 years old, since an olive regrows from its base and a trunk is never the tree's age. Another Athens olive carries an estimate spanning 300 to 2,500 years. Crete claims outright: the Olive Tree of Vouves is put at 2,000 to 4,000 years and still bears fruit, and a second, at Azoria, carries 3,000 to 3,400 years from pottery buried in its roots. All three say so plainly, which is more than most places manage. Twenty trees so far.

countries.name: Hungary
countries.intro: Budapest argues about its trees in public and keeps the evidence. The Old Acacia of Szechenyi Square is celebrated as 227 years old, planted in 1789, and a historian has taken that number apart using photographs of the square. The Taban Mulberry is credited to Ottoman occupiers by popular legend and, in the better sourced version, to Maria Theresa's eighteenth century push for a domestic silk industry, which put mulberry orchards across the district specifically to feed silkworms. Some dates are firm. Archduke Joseph, Palatine of Hungary, planted the Tree of Science with his own hands in 1823, on what was then his private island. Others come with a warning attached: the Seven Chieftains Plane is not the tree the name first belonged to. Twelve trees, one city so far.

countries.name: Ireland
countries.intro: Ireland's oldest trees are yews on old church ground, and nearly everything else worth the walk was shipped in by Victorians. Cork's Witch's Yew is put at more than 600 years and was voted the country's Tree of the Year in 2019, then backed by 11,372 people across Europe for the continental title; Dublin's Dean's Tree matches it for age. The rest of Dublin reads as a nineteenth century plant collection: Glasnevin's Atlas cedar, dawn redwood and Caucasian elm, the last of which a nurseryman propagated into a cultivar sold under the garden's own name, and a giant sequoia Queen Victoria planted on what is now presidential ground in 1861. Trinity College has the one nobody forgets, a plane slowly swallowing a cast iron bench. Two cities so far, 30 trees.

countries.name: Italy
countries.intro: Padua's botanical garden opened in 1545 and one of its founding plants is still alive: a dwarf fan palm that Goethe wrote an entire essay about in 1786, using it to illustrate his theory of how plants grow. That tree sets Italy's pattern. Its oldest survivors stand less in open woodland than behind walls someone built on purpose, villa gardens, monastery cloisters, university botanical collections kept for study rather than shade. Rome's own oldest confirmed tree, a 425-year-old oriental plane, grows in a garden laid out for a cardinal. Italy's national tree register lists more monumental specimens than any other country mapped here, but carries no age field at all, so most of the dates on this site come from regional catalogues and city archives instead, the same close reading that first put a number on Goethe's palm.

countries.name: Japan
countries.intro: Japan is the one country on this map where the oldest trees are older than the buildings by design. Shrines are rebuilt, sometimes every twenty years as a matter of ritual, while the tree in the courtyard is left alone and wrapped in a straw rope to mark it as sacred. A camphor at a shrine gate is not decoration, it is the thing the shrine was built around. The state has protected trees as Natural Monuments since 1919, and the Environment Ministry keeps a record of every tree in the country over three metres in girth, which is why ages and measurements here are firmer than almost anywhere else in Europe. Be careful with the biggest numbers all the same: a thousand years is usually tradition rather than measurement, and the sources say so. Some places here hold one tree, which was the whole reason to travel.

countries.name: Lithuania
countries.intro: Ancient Trees maps 8 places and 28 trees across Lithuania, most of them protected by a single Environment Ministry order rather than a city ordinance: one order, issued on one day in April 2018, designated five trees at once around the small town of Priekulė. The country's oldest confirmed tree, the Peace Hill Oak above the Kaunas reservoir, carries a name and role handed down from an earlier 800-year-old oak that a 2007 arson attack finally destroyed; Trainiškis does the same for a tree lost to a 2016 storm, mapping the honest young clone planted at its stump rather than pretending it is what it replaced. Braziūkai's Motinėlė, the country's thickest recorded lime trunk, sheltered insurgents against Russian rule in 1863, and Raudonė's seven-trunked lime was voted Lithuania's Tree of the Year in 2018. Lithuania protects its trees by decree; it does not always know how old they are.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.intro: The Netherlands is the wrong country for ancient trees and has them anyway. Half of it was seabed, peat bog or open water within the last thousand years, the soil is young, the water table sits close under the roots, and North Sea storms arrive with nothing in the way to slow them down. What survived did so under shelter, and that shapes the entire list: a pear tree inside an almshouse courtyard, a cycad potted in a botanical garden in 1704 and never repotted since, lindens pollarded for three centuries because a village square needed its shade. Dutch ancient trees are tended survivors rather than forest giants, which is why so many stand behind a gate you have to find rather than out in open parkland. It also explains the oldest one on this list: a fruit tree.

countries.name: Poland
countries.intro: Poland names some of its oldest trees after people, not always the ones you might expect. Krakow's Henryk Oak is named for a man who lived beside it from 1923 to 2010 and saved it from a wartime felling order, though the tree predates him by a century, the last survivor of a forest the village grew up around. Warsaw's oldest carries a grander name and an honest gap: Dab Mieszko I, six hundred to six hundred forty years old, is named for the ruler who brought Poland into recorded history, though it began growing centuries after his death. It survived a 2019 arson attack and stands propped and cabled, one of the last fragments of wild forest inside the city. Beyond the five original cities, a dozen national and continental champion trees each stand as their own destination, from a disputed 800-year-old yew at Ksiaz castle to Lodz's 2023 European Tree of the Year. Seventeen places are mapped so far, running centuries younger than equivalents further west, less for lack of old ground than a twentieth century that spared little of it.

countries.name: Portugal
countries.intro: Portugal has been putting individual trees on a legal register since 1938, and the habit shows. A tree of public interest here comes with a file: species, girth, height, the year it was classified, and often the year it was last measured, all published by the forestry institute. That makes Portuguese ages more reliable than most, and it makes the disagreements visible when they happen. The trees themselves are a record of the voyages, as in Spain but more so: jacarandas from Brazil, dragon trees from Madeira, Moreton Bay figs whose aerial roots turn a Lisbon garden into something that looks borrowed from another continent. Lisbon holds more classified trees than any other municipality in the country, which is unusual for a capital and says something about what the city chose to keep.

countries.name: Slovakia
countries.intro: Slovakia's most-told tree story belongs to Bojnice, where a linden behind the castle is tied by tradition to a visit from King Matthias Corvinus and put at over 700 years, no measurement behind the round number. The better-documented tree is a plainer oak in Dubinné, near Bardejov, hollow enough that the wood which would date it has rotted away, leaving a working estimate of at least 800 years and the country's own claim to its oldest oak. Most of the rest of the oldest trees here are lindens, which is not a coincidence: the lime has been Slovakia's national tree since the 13th century. Hronsek's stand in the yard of a UNESCO wooden church; Uzovská Panica keeps something rarer, a 250-year-old service tree that once marked a property line. Bratislava's own collection reads almost as an inventory of other continents: a Japanese pagoda tree on the Danube embankment, an Empress tree from China, a paper birch that belongs in Canada. 27 trees across 18 places now, and the plainest one, not the castle linden, is the oldest.

countries.name: Spain
countries.intro: Spain's great native trees are out in the countryside, in the dehesas where holm oaks stand a hundred paces apart over grazing pigs. What grows in its cities came back on ships. The ombu in Seville is from the Argentine pampas, the dragon trees are Canarian, the Moreton Bay figs are Australian and the ahuehuetes are Mexican, and they are here because Seville and Cadiz held the monopoly on trade with the Americas and captains brought seedlings home the way other people bring back souvenirs. The result is that a Spanish city garden is a record of where its ships went. It also explains the ages: most of these trees arrived with the botanical fashion of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, so two hundred years is old here and five hundred is exceptional.

countries.name: Sweden
countries.intro: Sweden's old trees survived on paperwork. Five of the ten mapped here are boundary oaks, oaks that marked where one property ended and the next began, which made felling one a legal problem rather than a morning's work. Four of them stand in Orgryte in Gothenburg and were declared nature monuments on the same day, 14 October 2025, after a citizens' group spent years pointing out that a crash barrier was growing into the largest one. That tree, Granseken, is over six metres round and at least five hundred years old. Stockholm's are royal rather than legal: Birger Jarl's Oak at around eight hundred years, Prince Eugen's on the Waldemarsudde grounds, and the elms of Kungstradgarden, which are only two centuries old and famous anyway, because in 1971 people sat in them to stop a metro entrance and won. The oldest thing on this page is not an oak at all. Old Tjikko is a thin, wind-bent spruce on the Fulufjallet plateau whose visible trunk is a few centuries old and whose root system has been carbon dated at roughly 9,550 years. Fifteen trees so far, across Gothenburg, Stockholm and Fulufjallet.

countries.name: Switzerland
countries.intro: Geneva has recorded the date a chestnut tree opens its first leaf every spring since 1818, one of the longest continuous records of its kind anywhere, and the tree currently doing the job is about eleven years old. The sautier of the cantonal parliament walks to the designated tree, checks it, and reports the date to the press. Age here tends to arrive with that sort of paperwork: five planes in the botanical garden were already mature enough to appear on a cantonal map in 1728, and the cedars of Parc Beaulieu, around 290 years old, grew from seed a French naturalist carried out of an English garden. Zurich adds four more, and Robenhausen contributes a single oak on the shore where a 19th-century dig gave a whole period of European prehistory its name. Twenty-six trees, three cities.

countries.name: Taiwan
countries.intro:
Taiwan's oldest trees are almost all conifers found deep in mountain forest rather than in a city park, on slopes too steep for the logging that cleared most of the island's lowland giants. The Bilu Sacred Tree, a Taiwan fir put at over 3,000 years, and the Sianglin Sacred Tree, a red cypress whose age is disputed between a newly measured 626 years and a long-quoted 2,300, both stand alone in remote reserve forest rather than beside any town.

Chishang's contribution is deliberately different: a fifty-year-old Bishop wood known not for its age but for a shampoo advertisement filmed beneath it in 2001, which turned an ordinary field tree into one of the island's most visited photo stops. Taipei holds the rest of what is mapped so far: a three-hundred-year-old camphor at Zhishan Rock, a stand of Ryukyu pines known as the Common Three Pines, junipers planted at the Confucius Temple in 1962, and a ginkgo on a university campus. Between them they cover most of what an ancient tree can be here, from a shrine-grove giant nobody has fully aged to a tree made famous by something that happened to it decades after it was already grown.

countries.name: Turkey
countries.intro: Istanbul's oldest living thing is an oriental plane put at 1,300 to 1,400 years, which predates the city's Ottoman name by seven centuries. It stands inside a university forestry station at Bahcekoy, and a stranger one grows nearby: the Ahtapot Cinar, whose lowest branches touched the ground centuries ago, thickened where they landed, and now read as seven trunks sharing a single root system. Turkey keeps a national Monument Tree register that carries ages, so the numbers here are firmer than in most of Europe. The famous exception is Topkapi's plane in the First Courtyard, the one said to have witnessed the conquest of 1453, which has been dead for about a century. Fifteen trees mapped, all in Istanbul, and eight of them are planes.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.intro: Britain's oldest trees are yews, and it is churches, not palaces, that kept most of them standing. London's Totteridge Yew is put at two thousand years old, roughly a millennium and a half older than the church built beside it, one of many British yews reckoned to predate Christianity in these islands. Oaks tell a different story: a mild, fire-free climate let them stand long enough to earn names tied to real dates, a Domesday Oak already growing when the Conquest was surveyed in 1086, a Royal Oak enclosed inside a park wall in 1637 because it was already centuries old. Age here survives less through law than inheritance, a landed estate, a cathedral close, a royal park that changed hands but never changed use. Twenty-four places are mapped so far, from Edinburgh's botanic garden to Oxford's college quadrangles, and wherever a yew appears it tends to win on age. The extreme case is Fortingall, a Perthshire village of a few houses whose churchyard yew is dated at anywhere between two thousand and five thousand years, because the heartwood rotted away centuries ago and there is nothing left to count.

countries.name: United States
countries.intro: America's most famous trees are destinations rather than city sights. People drive to the Angel Oak outside Charleston and to the Hundred-Horse Chestnut's American cousins the way they drive to a canyon, and that is how this country reads on a map of old trees. The registers behind them are patchy in a way that surprised us: Portland keeps a genuine Heritage Tree list and Hawaii designates individual Exceptional Trees by county ordinance, while Philadelphia, Charleston, Seattle, San Francisco and Savannah have no curated list at all. They either protect any tree over a set trunk size automatically, or they publish every street tree they own and nothing in between. So the good American trees are found one at a time, by name, and that is how we map them.

species.name: Aleppo Pine
species.intro: An Aleppo pine keeps its cones locked shut on the branch for years and opens them with heat, so the fire that kills the tree sows the next generation of it. That trick is why a nineteenth century engineer bet a whole hillside on the species. When Nice became French in 1860 the slopes of Mont Boron were bare rock, and the replanting begun in 1862 is the pine forest you walk through today. The other four are city trees. Rome's grows in the Villa Celimontana, one of two officially monumental trees standing within a few metres of each other. Madrid's, about 150 years old, is in the Campo del Moro under the west front of the Royal Palace. Barcelona's, at about 122, is in the Torre Girona gardens, and Florence's stands on Via Giramondino. Five cities, all of them Mediterranean, which for this pine is simply home.

species.name: American Elm
species.intro: Central Park's western edge once carried about 500 American elms. A New York Times survey counted 23 of them in 1985, and one of the four trees mapped here is on that shortlist, standing on Central Park West opposite the natural history museum and wider than it is tall. Dutch elm disease reached the city in the 1930s and took the great majority of the elms that had shaded nearly every street in it, which is why every survivor now reads as an event. A pair east of the Mall grow straight out of exposed Manhattan schist, roots spread flat across rock over a billion years old. The avenue on the Mall itself has been replanted three times, because foot traffic kept compacting the soil, and the row you walk under now went in during the 1920s. All four are in Central Park.

species.name: American Sycamore
species.intro: Europe mostly grows this tree as half of another one. Platanus occidentalis is the sycamore of the eastern United States and the American parent of the London plane, the hybrid that lines half the streets in Europe, so a full grown specimen standing in its own right is unusual here. Ljubljana has two, and they are the last of an avenue that ran from the foot of the castle out toward the Dolenjska road, drawn on a map of the city in 1744 and gone everywhere else since. Both are individually listed as natural values of national importance, which almost nothing in the historic centre is. The thicker one is 596 centimetres round and 33 metres tall. Como's is the same height and the tallest tree on the lakefront walk, with no age, no planting date and no record of who put it there.

species.name: Amur Cork Tree
species.intro: You can press a thumb into the bark of this tree and it gives. The Amur cork tree carries a thick, soft, deeply ridged corky layer that dents under a hand and springs back, and Munich's natural monument ordinance protects its specimen for exactly that, an interesting bark pattern, while calling the species extremely rare in the city. Under the cork the inner bark is a startling sulphur yellow, and it is one of the fundamental herbs of Chinese medicine. Paris's went into a small garden opposite the Collège de France in 1925 and wears a lightning scar down the trunk. Washington's stand inside the Roosevelt Memorial with no provenance at all: in 1962 the Park Service went looking for a planting record, found none, and kept the trees on the grounds that they were, in its own words, very attractive old trees.

species.name: Atlas Cedar
species.intro: An Atlas cedar in a European park is safer than one at home. Cedrus atlantica grows wild in a narrow band of mountains in Morocco and Algeria, and the IUCN now lists the species as endangered there, squeezed by drought, logging and a warming climate its range cannot outrun. In a nineteenth century garden it has none of those problems, which is why the eleven mapped here are mostly enormous and mostly untroubled. Lyon's is the reason its park has the shape it does, with the lawn and paths arranged to give the tree room rather than the other way round. Perugia's took the weight of a trumpeter and an accordionist playing a concert twelve metres up in its crown in 2020. Lucca's carries the name of a priest who from 1943 hid Jews and partisans in his community's house. Nine cities so far.

species.name: Austrian Pine
species.intro: Austrian pine, Pinus nigra, is a Mediterranean and Balkan species that nineteenth-century cities across two continents planted for exactly what it does best: shrug off compacted, disturbed ground that would stunt almost anything else. Montreal's specimen, just inside the gate of Notre-Dame-des-Neiges cemetery, took that tolerance sideways instead of up, spreading eighteen metres wide on a trunk barely half as tall, shaped more like a mushroom than a pine. Portland's grows out of a street planter a florist put in before the street existed, in the 1870s or 80s, and has since reached 31 metres. Vienna's stands in a small park named for the writer Marie von Ebner-Eschenbach, protected as a natural monument since 1942 with no age ever recorded, an unusually thin file for a tree the city thought worth the paperwork. None of the three needed anything resembling good soil to get old.

species.name: Avocado
species.intro:
Persea americana is native to central Mexico and grown almost everywhere in Europe for its fruit rather than its shade, which makes a mature specimen remarkable rather than ordinary. The site has three mapped.

Malaga's, in a working school courtyard in Churriana, is the oldest at over 150 years and one of the first avocados ever brought to Spain, planted decades before Malaga and neighbouring Granada became the source of nine in every ten avocados sold in the country today. Barcelona has two, both catalogued for height rather than fruit: one 17 metres tall in Les Corts, planted in 1945, and a second at Teatre Lliure, older than the theatre building beside it by more than half a century.

None of the three is grown commercially. All three simply outgrew the fruit tree anyone expected them to stay.

species.name: Bald Cypress
species.intro: Bald cypress grows with its feet in standing water in Louisiana and Florida, pushing woody knees up out of the mud around its trunk. Every one mapped here stands on dry European ground. Nineteenth century gardeners wanted the shape and took the swamp tree without the swamp, and it obliged: the pair behind a wall in Bergamo have been there more than two centuries, and the one in the Charlottenburg palace garden in Berlin about the same. Seville built its monument to the Romantic poet Becquer around a bald cypress that had been growing on the spot first and had nothing to do with him. Milan's was filed under the wrong genus for years, called a metasequoia by the gardeners looking after it, until somebody checked properly. Seven trees, seven cities, and no city has two.

species.name: Baobab
species.intro: Adansonia digitata belongs to the dry savannah of Africa, where it stores water in a swollen trunk and can live a thousand years. Nothing here is that old; what the three mapped specimens share is how fast the trunk gets there. Honolulu's Foster Garden tree, nicknamed the Dead Rat Tree for its grey, furred seed pods, reached a girth close to thirteen metres in around ninety years. Singapore's, near Melati Gate, was already five metres round when it was endorsed as a heritage tree in 2016 at just thirty. The third, on the University of Hawaii's Manoa campus, is loved enough that when Gilmore Hall was demolished in 1973 the university built its replacement Art Building around the baobab rather than move it; the university calls it the largest baobab in the United States. None has been in the ground a century, and all three already look ancient.

species.name: Bishop Wood
species.intro: Bischofia javanica is planted as an ordinary street and avenue tree across the tropics, which makes the trees mapped here unusual simply for how old they have been allowed to get. Okinawa calls the species akagi and has treated old specimens as sacred for generations: the grove at Shuri Kinjo was designated a national natural monument on 15 May 1972, the exact day Okinawa reverted to Japan, and the prefecture's own note says plainly that most akagi this size around the old castle were lost before that; at Uchima, a single akagi stands over a village well and has been the site of community festivals for as long as anyone remembers. Porto's contribution is quieter but still striking: three of the oldest bischofia documented in Portugal grow together in one botanical garden, kept and classified as trees of public interest rather than replaced. Three mapped so far, across two countries.

species.name: Bitter Orange
species.intro: Citrus aurantium is too sour to eat off the tree, which is exactly why it survived where sweeter oranges would have been picked bare: it was planted for shade, symmetry and scent rather than fruit. Its home in this data is the ablutions courtyards of Andalusia's great mosques, later absorbed whole into the cathedrals built over them. Cordoba's Patio de los Naranjos is the grove that gives the type its name here, ninety-eight trees in rows lined up with the prayer hall's columns, watered by channels that trace back to a tenth-century cistern; oranges are recorded growing in it since at least 1512, replanted tree by tree ever since, so the grid is ancient and no single trunk is. Seville Cathedral's own Patio de los Naranjos looks the same age but is not: a twentieth-century restoration replanted it, whatever grew there before did not survive. And in the Real Alcázar a single stunted bitter orange carries the name of Pedro the Cruel with no record of when it was planted or why, which the page states plainly rather than guessing.

species.name: Black Locust
species.intro: The oldest tree in Paris is a black locust planted in 1601, and the second oldest is its son. Jean Robin, herbalist to Henri IV, raised the first from seed sent out of the Appalachians; in 1636 his son Vespasien took a cutting and planted it in the new royal medicinal garden two kilometres away. Both are still standing, and the genus Robinia carries the family name. The species is otherwise the opposite of distinguished. It arrived from North America in the eighteenth century, spread across Europe's sandy ground so successfully that it is now valued mainly for holding loose banks together, and it typically runs up thin and fast and then falls over.
