Which is what makes the exceptions worth the walk: Barcelona's went sideways to 4.3 metres on twelve metres of tree, and Antwerp's is the thickest recorded anywhere in Belgium.

species.name: Black Mulberry
species.intro: Britain's silk industry failed on a species error and left the trees behind. In 1608 James I ordered mulberries planted across the country to feed silkworms, but silkworms eat white mulberry and mostly refuse black, and black was what went into the ground. Charlton House got one of them and it is still fruiting four centuries later. Christ's College in Cambridge planted another in 1608 or 1609, the year after John Milton was born, and it is now reckoned at 417 years. Nothing here will look large. Mulberries do not build thick trunks, which is why Belgium's national champion measures 1.28 metres around and reads as unremarkable beside almost anything else in the same park. Breda's public library was designed around three of them rather than the other way round. Eight mapped, in five cities, and four of the eight are in London.

species.name: Black Poplar
species.intro: Europe's native black poplar has been quietly bred out of its own landscape. Almost every poplar planted along a European road or river for the last two centuries has been a hybrid with an American species, so the wild form is now one of the continent's more threatened natives, and it is fast, soft and short lived on top of that. Very few reach the size of the four here. Bordeaux's has the biggest waistline in the city's entire register at 741 centimetres, three trunks fused near the ground, though its two official descriptions disagree about its height by twelve metres. Trento's made the city's monumental list in 2024 at 570 centimetres and carries no age anywhere. Venice's grows alone in a wood that took over a former military firing range on the Certosa. Setubal's pair stand beside the school named for the poet Bocage.

species.name: Black Walnut
species.intro: Budapest's biggest black walnut is also its frailest, and both findings come out of the same survey. The city's parks company dated the tree on Margaret Island to around 213 years in 2020 and measured its trunk as the thickest black walnut there by a wide margin, with the runner-up 119 centimetres smaller around; a national database ranks it second in Hungary on girth. Portland's is what is left of a fourteen acre estate, a single walnut on a school lawn, and its own plaque and the city's field guide disagree about the planting date by roughly fifteen years. Split's is a curiosity for a different reason: Juglans nigra is an eastern North American forest tree, and the city's botanical survey grades it a rarity precisely because it has no business making a living this far down the Adriatic.

species.name: Blue Jacaranda
species.intro: For a few weeks a year a jacaranda stops looking like any other tree, its whole crown turning violet-blue and the ground beneath carpeting in the same colour when the flowers drop, which is why cities from Pretoria to Sydney planted it far outside its native Argentina and Bolivia. Cagliari's specimen in the Giardini Pubblici does this every May among trees chosen for shade rather than spectacle. Cordoba's grew inside a walled garden that belonged first to a Dominican convent and then to a Renaissance palace, invisible from the street until the gate finally opened to the public in 2004. Sydney's is the odd one out: the jacaranda that made the University of Sydney's Quadrangle famous fell in 2016 after 88 years, and the tree standing there now is a clone planted the following year, carrying the same genetics and almost none of the age.

species.name: Boab
species.intro: Australia's boab is the only baobab outside Africa and Madagascar, a swollen bottle-trunked tree that drops its leaves for the dry season and photosynthesises through its bark. Its scientific name, Adansonia gregorii, comes from Ferdinand von Mueller naming it after Augustus Gregory, whose 1855 expedition camped beside the Timber Creek tree that still carries the party's carved arrival and departure dates. Derby's so-called Boab Prison Tree carries a legend, colonial prisoners held inside it, that historians have traced to a 1948 newspaper caption rather than any record; what is documented is its real use by the Nyikina and Warrwa people as shelter and burial ground. And Perth's Gija Jumulu, over 750 years old, made the longest recorded road journey of any living tree its size: 3,200km from the Kimberley in 2008, given its name by the Gija people who once stood beside it at home.

species.name: Bodhi Tree
species.intro: Most of these trees have a planting date, because with a bodhi the lineage is the point. Cuttings are carried from tree to tree back toward Bodh Gaya, and Thai temples record the year one arrived the way they record a relic. Wat Saket's went in in 1818, brought home by two monks sent abroad by King Rama II who came back after three years with cuttings instead of the relics they were sent for. Wat Phra Kaew's dates from 1864 and grows inside the most photographed temple complex in Thailand, where almost nobody photographs it. Wat Benchamabophit's was planted in 1900, nine years after Thailand received its first direct cutting from Bodh Gaya itself. The fourth in Bangkok is Lan Pho on the lawn at Thammasat University, where the protest that brought down a dictatorship began in October 1973. Singapore's stands on Pearl's Hill.

species.name: Bottle Tree
species.intro: Brachychiton populneus carries a name it barely earns. Kurrajong is what Australians call it at home; the English "bottle tree" nickname borrows from Brachychiton rupestris, its barrel-trunked cousin, but this species keeps a slimmer, upright shape its whole life. Three planted specimens map here, all in old botanic and garden collections rather than in the wild. Caserta's, in a Bourbon queen's English Garden, has reached thirty-five metres, roughly twice the height the species usually manages. Barcelona's grows half-hidden in the wooded part of the Torre Girona gardens, the one tree here a visitor actually has to go looking for. Valencia's is a garden's second bottle tree by name only, sharing a nickname with an unrelated species and nothing else.

species.name: Box Elder
species.intro: Box elder has a bad reputation. It seeds itself into alleys and vacant lots, drops limbs without warning, hosts the boxelder bugs that swarm into houses every autumn, and rarely gets the chance to grow old before someone cuts it down as a weed. It is also, unusually for a maple, compound-leafed: where every other Acer carries a single lobed leaf, this one splits its into three, five or seven separate leaflets, so people routinely mistake it for an ash. Three trees on this site are the exceptions that outlasted the reputation. Chicago's, on a public golf course in Edgebrook, is Illinois's state champion by the University of Illinois Extension's own scoring formula, undated but the biggest known in the state. Eindhoven's stands in a small parish churchyard, planted in the 1920s, and has outlived the congregation that put it there. Setubal's, at roughly 117 years old, is the oldest living thing in the city's main park, on ground that was open countryside when it was planted.

species.name: Buddhist Pine
species.intro: The Buddhist pine is not a pine. Podocarpus macrophyllus is a broad-leaved conifer from Japan and southern China, and the trees mapped here show how differently the same species ends up living. At Kakuonji in Kamakura, past where the tourist route gives up, one grows as a City Natural Monument in the quiet inner precinct of a temple most visitors never reach. In Naples, Piazza Cavour holds a pair: the register only recognises the upright one, 25 metres tall, because its twin toppled years ago and kept growing horizontally, struck from the official list for lying down rather than for dying. In Las Vegas it turns up as ordinary landscaping, pressed flat against a wall on the UNLV campus, and happens to be the state's largest recorded specimen anyway. A temple guardian, a survivor lying on its side, and a state record hiding as a hedge plant. Three mapped so far.

species.name: Bunya Pine
species.intro: The bunya pine drops the heaviest cone of any conifer on earth: up to ten kilograms, roughly a bowling ball, from a crown that can be twenty-eight metres up. In southeast Queensland, the only place it grows wild, the trees fruit heavily every few years, and Aboriginal groups travelled hundreds of kilometres for the gatherings that followed. Australian parks now sign and fence them for the obvious reason. Europe planted them for the silhouette instead: a straight column with branches in flat symmetrical whorls and leaves stiff enough to draw blood. Porto's is the tallest thing in the Jardim da Cordoaria at roughly 40 metres. Bucaco's is five metres round beside a hotel that was still a Carmelite convent when it was planted. Barcelona's has been in the Teatre Grec gardens since about 1920.

species.name: Bur Oak
species.intro: Four of these five were standing before Chicago was. The bur oak is the prairie oak, its bark thick enough to survive the grass fires that once kept the Midwest open, so the old ones left in the city are survivors of the savanna it was built across. One in the grove on Wooded Island blew down around 2016 and its rings were counted back to roughly 1730. The oldest in the Union Ridge Cemetery savanna is put at 325 to 375 years. The oak on the Midway Plaisance was left standing when everything around it was cleared and regraded for the 1893 World's Fair. Local history makes a fourth a witness tree the Potawatomi used to find the route back to the Des Plaines River. Washington's is the exception: Frederick Law Olmsted Jr. kept it in the 1930s while clearing about 250 trees out of Union Square.

species.name: California Fan Palm
species.intro: Everyone in Athens will tell you Queen Amalia planted the palms at the National Garden entrance. The calendar disagrees. Amalia laid the garden out between 1838 and 1840 and left Greece for good in 1862, and Washingtonia filifera did not reach European cultivation until seed arrived at a Belgian nursery around 1876, three years before the genus was even named. The row went in later, and her name attached itself the way a founder's name does. None of that makes the palms less worth the walk. Nice's stand at the corners of three formal flowerbeds at the Villa Masséna, designed by Édouard André and opened to the public in 1921 on a condition attached to the bequest. Barcelona's four have been in the courtyard of a former orphanage since about 1904. The species itself comes from desert oases in the American Southwest and northern Mexico.

species.name: Camperdown Elm
species.intro: Every Camperdown elm alive is the same tree. Around 1835 a forester on the Earl of Camperdown's estate near Dundee found a young elm growing contorted and weeping instead of upright, and because the mutation will not come from seed, every specimen since has been a cutting grafted onto a straight trunked host. Brooklyn has two of them. The famous one went in behind Prospect Park's Boathouse in 1872 and had declined so badly by the 1960s that the poet Marianne Moore wrote in its defence; the second stands two miles south in Green-Wood, and nobody recorded when. Edinburgh's grows by the main door of St Cuthbert's, a parish site far older than the 1894 building on it. Three are mapped, and none of them has a straight branch anywhere.

species.name: Camphor Tree
species.intro: Crush a camphor leaf and the tree explains itself: the sharp medicinal scent is camphor, distilled for centuries from its wood, and it is one reason the species lives so long, discouraging the insects and fungi that hollow out other trees. In Japan the kusunoki is the great shrine tree, wrapped in sacred rope, its canopy sometimes wider than the buildings it shelters; several of the country's largest and oldest trees are camphors, and city districts have been rerouted around them. The species is evergreen, so a thousand-year camphor in January looks as alive as it does in June. The camphor trees mapped so far are listed oldest first, shrine giants leading.

species.name: Canadian Poplar
species.intro: The oldest poplar in the Netherlands grows behind a concert hall in Arnhem, on the last stretch of moat the city never filled in, and it is not supposed to have got this far. Canadian poplar is a hybrid of Europe's black poplar and an American cottonwood, bred for timber and shelter belts, fast, soft and finished within decades rather than centuries. Arnhem's has stood since somewhere between 1750 and 1800. The other three are dated in decades, and what makes them worth the walk is what happened around them. Warsaw's was already mature when the ground it stands on became a transit camp in 1944. Den Bosch's went in around 1941, under occupation, and was a young tree when the fighting reached the city. Antwerp's is simply enormous, 35 metres with six metres of clear trunk before the crown starts.

species.name: Canary Island Date Palm
species.intro: Every Canary Island date palm on the French Riviera arguably descends from one garden on Nice's eastern port, where Baron Vigier is said to have acclimatised the species in France for the first time in 1864. That rests on the garden's own preservation society rather than on any independent record, so take it as the claim it is. The species is easy to admire and impossible to date, because a palm lays down no growth rings to count. Valencia's Palacio de Pineda has a construction date to the year, 1728 to 1731, and its palm has nothing at all; you can order a coffee under it. Barcelona's double row along the Vil.la Amelia avenue produces its own small disagreement, since the city register counts fourteen palms and the garden's chronicler counts fifteen. Valencia's other three stand in a row so recognisable that a bar took their nickname.

species.name: Canary Pine
species.intro: Pinus canariensis is endemic to the Canary Islands and about as fire-adapted as a pine gets: a mature tree can resprout new needles directly from a trunk that fire has scorched black, a trick almost no other pine in the world manages, which is how specimens survive centuries on slopes that burn periodically. The two most extreme examples stand 150 metres apart above the town of Vilaflor de Chasna on Tenerife, on the same short marked trail off the TF-21. Pino Gordo is on the town's own coat of arms, 9.36 metres round at the trunk and the thickest native tree in Spain, estimated at 700 to 800 years old, already a substantial pine when Castile finished conquering the island in 1496. Pino de las Dos Pernadas, the taller and slimmer half of the pair at 56 metres, is the tallest native tree in Spain, its trunk splitting about ten metres up into two near-identical limbs, which is what its name literally describes. Both carry visible fire scars and both are free to reach on foot from the same car park. The third, in Seville, is a different kind of specimen entirely: an undated pine on the open grounds of the university's engineering campus, rated in optimal health by the city's 2022 survey of singular trees, standing 26 metres tall a very long way from the volcanic slopes the species calls home.

species.name: Cannon Ball Tree
species.intro: Couroupita guianensis grows its fruit and flowers straight out of the trunk rather than the branches, a habit botanists call cauliflory and gardens call a hazard: ripe cannonball-sized fruit falls from height and splits open with a smell that carries, and Honolulu's Foster Garden has posted a sign warning visitors under its specimen. Three trees on this site share the trick. Singapore's, in the Ginger Garden, grew from seed E.J.H. Corner carried aboard ship in 1931 during an eight-hour stop in Ceylon. Its flowers make no nectar; the sterile pollen at their centre exists only to bring carpenter bees in for the fertile kind elsewhere on the bloom. Oahu's second specimen, on the UH Manoa campus, carries a trunk 314 centimetres round and an unconfirmed campus legend that the playwright Thornton Wilder planted it in 1933. All three flower and fruit from bark most trees keep bare.

species.name: Cappadocian Maple
species.intro: Acer cappadocicum takes its name from Cappadocia, the region of central Anatolia where it grows wild in the mountains, though its native range continues north into the Caucasus, which is why it is sometimes called Colchis maple instead, after the kingdom Jason sailed for in the story of the Golden Fleece. Snap a leaf stalk on any of the three mapped here and the sap that beads up is milky white rather than clear, the same trick its close relative the Norway maple plays. What gardeners actually plant it for is the autumn show: rather than the mixed reds and oranges of most maples, this one turns a uniform, saturated gold and holds the colour for weeks. Cork's grows in the gardens at Blarney Castle, dated to somewhere between one and one and a half centuries old by a 2009 heritage survey that never recorded who planted it. Utrecht's stands at the west entrance to Wilhelminapark, one of the park's original 1880s plantings according to the Dutch national monumental tree register. Lyon's, in the Tête d'Or's arboretum since the garden was founded in 1857, has been measured at 3.20 metres round and 26 metres tall, mature rather than record-breaking. None of the three carries a confirmed planting date, which for a tree grown as a specimen rather than a landmark is the ordinary state of things.

species.name: Caucasian Elm
species.intro: Europe lost most of its large elms to a fungus in the twentieth century, and these survived by not quite being elms. Zelkova carpinifolia is an elm relative from the mountain forests between the Black Sea and the Caspian, far less susceptible to Dutch elm disease, which is why trees this size still stand in the Latin Quarter and along the Avenue Foch. The shape gives it away: a short trunk breaking into a dense sheaf of near vertical stems, so the crown reads as a bundle held upright rather than a spreading canopy. Oxford's is the tallest recorded anywhere in Britain at around 33 metres. Dublin's was propagated into a named cultivar sold under the garden's own name. Florence's lost roughly two thirds of its height to surgery in the 1980s and is still on the national register. Ten are mapped, and only Paris has two.

species.name: Caucasian Wingnut
species.intro: The Caucasian wingnut is a walnut relative from the humid forests between the Black and Caspian Seas, and Amsterdam has more remarkable ones than almost any city outside its native range. It reached Europe around 1782 and thrives in exactly the wet, soft ground that much of the Dutch capital is built on. In summer it hangs curtains of green winged seeds, the catkins that give it its name, sometimes half a metre long. Left alone it suckers into a small grove from a single tree, which is why several of the city's specimens read as thickets rather than trunks. Amsterdammers have gone to court to keep them: one felling permit fight over a pair of wingnuts ran all the way to the Raad van State, the country's highest administrative court. These are the wingnuts mapped on the site so far.

species.name: Cedar of Lebanon
species.intro: This is the only tree on a national flag, and the only one whose timber built both Solomon's temple and the ships of the Phoenicians, at least according to the sources those builders left behind. When seeds reached Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries the Cedar of Lebanon became the ultimate estate status symbol: an aristocrat planted one knowing only his grandchildren would see the famous silhouette, the enormous level layers of dark foliage held out flat as trays. That slow flat-topped shape is the tree's signature and takes a century to appear, so every convincing cedar crown you see is old almost by definition. The cedars mapped so far stand in parks and former estates, oldest first.

species.name: Cherry
species.intro: Three cherries on this map carry only their genus, Prunus, most cherry trees being finished inside a century, which makes each of these an exception rather than the rule. Uda's Sen'nen-zakura is reckoned at over 900 years old, standing beside the stone steps up to the temple Butsuryuji. Fukuoka's Seicho-zakura was lifted whole by crane in January 2008, root ball and all, an eight-metre tree weighing roughly three and a half tonnes, and set down thirty metres from where it had grown. Kyoto's Kurumagaeshi-zakura, the carriage-turning cherry, takes its name from a story that an emperor's carriage once turned back rather than pass it; the tree there now is a roughly 80-year-old successor, not the original. If you know which of Japan's many flowering cherries any of these are, tell us.

species.name: Chilean Wine Palm
species.intro: The Chilean wine palm carries one of the thickest trunks in the palm family, a grey column that can run past three and a half metres round, and that trunk is why the species barely survives in the wild. Jubaea chilensis stores its sugar as sap, and for two centuries Chilean producers got at it by felling a mature palm and draining the stump for palm honey, a tapped tree never growing back. Central Chile's valleys once filled with these palms; a handful of protected stands are what is left. The tree found a second life in nineteenth-century Europe instead, where its rare cold-hardiness for a palm made it a prize for villa gardens built to look exotic in a climate that kills most others. Three of the ones mapped here still stand in exactly that ground, in Italian villa parks from Genoa to Florence.

species.name: Chinaberry
species.intro: Three cities, three uses for the same tree. Cordoba grew one to twenty-four and a half metres beside the Puerta de Almodovar, casting four hundred square metres of shade from a species that usually stops at ten; its hard seed stones, strung as rosary beads, gave the tree its other name, bead tree. Nara planted its specimen on the burned platform of Todai-ji's east pagoda, because chinaberry was believed to drive off evil spirits and was traditionally set at sites where the dead were remembered; for two weeks each May it covers itself in pale purple flowers. Paris keeps one in Square Boucicaut, where the French call it lilas de Perse, Persian lilac, and where its pale yellow berries stay on the bare branches through December and January, a Mediterranean tree fruiting through a cold it was never bred for.

species.name: Chinese Hackberry
species.intro: In Japan this tree is enoki, and for two and a half centuries it did a job before it did anything ornamental: the Tokugawa shogunate planted one, or a red pine, at every ichirizuka, the paired earthen mounds that marked each ri of the great highways out of Edo, so a traveller had shade to rest in as well as a distance to measure. Most of those mounds are gone; a few survive as protected sites with the tree still standing on them. Shrines took to the species for the same reason city wards do now: it grows fast, broad and long-lived, wide enough in the crown to be worth wrapping in a sacred rope when a shrine decides a tree has become its shintai. All three mapped so far are measured rather than dated, because Japan's local surveys record girth, height and crown spread as a 'pride tree' or giant-tree designation and leave age to whoever asks later: a Kyoto Imperial Palace gate hackberry with a canopy nearly ten metres wider than the tree is tall, a Nashinoki Shrine hackberry logged at 21 metres, and a Hiroshima shrine hackberry that quietly out-girths the celebrated camphor sharing its grounds. Three are mapped, in two cities.

species.name: Chinese Juniper
species.intro: The Chinese juniper is best known in the West as a bonsai subject, trained small in a tray. Left alone for centuries beside a temple or a palace, it does the opposite: it grows into a slow, twisting giant whose bark spirals hard enough that people read dragons into it. Every specimen mapped here earned a dragon story this way, from the coiled eastern branch at Seoul's Changdeokgung, which court records describe as a dragon ascending to heaven, to Beijing's Nine Dragon Cypress, misnamed a cypress by generations who never doubted the resemblance. Kamakura's pair at Kenchoji have stood since the temple's founding in 1253, on a site once known as Hell Valley. The species lives 600 to 750 years in these settings and rarely leaves them: courts and monasteries protected what everyone else would have shaped smaller. These are the Chinese junipers mapped so far, oldest first.

species.name: Chir Pine
species.intro: The chir pine belongs to the dry outer foothills of the Himalaya, the resin belt running from Pakistan through northern India into Nepal, where it is tapped for turpentine the way other trees are tapped for rubber. Its needles run up to thirty centimetres in bundles of three and hang rather than bristle, so a mature crown looks like a loose green waterfall rather than the stiff cone most people picture at the word pine. Every tree mapped so far is a long way from that range. Rome's monumental register lists exactly two: one on Colle Oppio, grown from a seed the Tibetologist Giuseppe Tucci carried back from an expedition and planted directly above Nero's buried Domus Aurea, the other in a 1930s neighbourhood park in Tuscolano. Hobart's stands in the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens' pinetum, planted when nineteenth-century foresters were testing which northern conifers would take to a southern hemisphere climate. Three cities, three transplants, none of them anywhere near where the species is actually common.

species.name: Coast Redwood
species.intro: The tallest tree species on earth takes a serious share of its water straight out of sea mist, which is the problem with growing it away from the northern Californian fog belt. Europe hands it the rainless summer and none of the fog. So the redwood on Rome's Pincio has stopped at thirty metres, a good height for a Roman tree and a failure for a species that passes 110 at home, and has gone thick instead, 4.2 metres around. Where the air stays damp the answer is different: the pair at Bucaco reach forty-five metres, and Lucca's clears every tower inside the walls except the two you can climb. Most went in within a couple of decades of each other, because seed reached Europe in the 1840s and every garden with ambition wanted one. Twelve are mapped, and no two of them share a city.

species.name: Common Camellia
species.intro: A camellia is supposed to drop its flower whole, head and all, which is why samurai were said to dislike them. The four hundred year old tree at Byakugo-ji in Nara does not: it sheds petal by petal, and it opens red, white, peach, striped and variegated blossoms on the same plant, which is how it became one of the three famous camellias of the city. The other three mapped here are Portuguese, and that is not an accident. The mild wet north of the country suited Camellia japonica so well that Portuguese growers ended up exporting it back to the rest of Europe. Porto has traded on that since the nineteenth century; the pair in front of the church at Paranhos are six and a half metres tall with crowns ten metres across, which is not what most people expect from a shrub in a pot.

species.name: Common Fig
species.intro: A common fig is a Mediterranean shrub that most gardens this far north keep low and trained flat against a warm wall. Three of these refused. Paris's, in the Square Georges Cain beside the Musee Carnavalet, stands ten metres tall in the open with a trunk 145 centimetres round, which a fig this far from the Mediterranean has no real business doing. London's Amwell Street fig went the other way, sprawling low across the front of a former parochial school in Clerkenwell on several stems from one rootstock, propped up where its own limbs outgrew their strength, and it may have been planted as a teaching aid rather than an ornament. Seville's is the oldest of the three at over 300 years, growing in the Huerto del Rey Moro, a walled plot on Calle Enladrillada that neighbours occupied in 2004 rather than watch it get built over, and have run themselves ever since. One species, three trees that each broke the pattern in a different way.

species.name: Common Lime
species.intro: Groningen's oldest tree is one of these, about 340 years old at a farmhouse called De Rollen, and so is the peace tree Antwerp planted on its Grote Markt on 3 September 1994. Common lime is a hybrid of Europe's two wild limes, and it took over the north as the tree you plant in rows: along canals, up drives, around squares. Most of the ones here are what is left of a row. Utrecht has a canal stretch named Onder de Linden, under the lindens, in the 17th century, and out at the Uithof a linden that went into the ground around 1750 when the land around it was farmland. The veteran at Clingendael in The Hague is the last member of a row that stopped being one long ago. Helsinki's is the thickest park lime in Finland, on an island in the city's harbour.

species.name: Cook Pine
species.intro: Cook pine comes from one stretch of the Pacific, New Caledonia's Isle of Pines, where eighteenth-century sailors mistook its narrow, leaning columns for stone and named the island after the mistake. Planted as an ornamental far from home, it tends to end up the tallest thing around: Brisbane's, one of two set out by Prince Albert, Duke of Edinburgh, in 1868, is now the tallest tree in the City Botanic Gardens at forty-five metres. Lima's stands inside a seventeenth-century Spanish olive grove and has already outgrown trees three centuries older than it. Palermo's rises thirty-eight metres over Villa Tasca's swan lake, the pine on one shore answering a fig tree's shade on the other.

species.name: Copper Beech
species.intro: Every copper beech in Europe descends from an accident. The purple leaf is a mutation that turns up at random in wild green beech forests, and it is a handicap rather than an advantage: the pigment masks the chlorophyll underneath and cuts the light the leaf can put to work, so purple seedlings are outgrown by green ones and vanish. The tree exists in numbers only because gardeners in German and Swiss forests found the freak worth keeping and propagated it, and because it does not come true from seed it is usually grafted. Leiden's was grafted low onto a green rootstock, and two centuries of mismatched growth rates have left it with a broad gnarled base that looks nothing like a beech. Boston's is the only living Historic Landmark in Cambridge, designated in 1985 to stop a building. Eleven cities hold the thirteen mapped here, from Portland to Porto.

species.name: Cork Oak
species.intro: A working cork oak gets stripped to the bare wood every nine years or so, its bark peeled off in slabs for wine corks and flooring. None of these five has ever been harvested, so they carry the thing the industry takes away: an outer bark up to thirty centimetres thick, spongy enough that pressing a thumb into it is half the reason to go. Caserta's is the one tree on that walk you can put a hand on and be surprised by. The oak in Rome's orangery has been measured twice in three years and grew in the interval, from 5.00 metres around in 2021 to 5.30. Sintra's is called the Sobreira dos Fetos, the Fern Cork Oak, because ferns grow straight out of its bark; Portugal's register puts it at 350 years. The other two stand in Florence and in the Bucaco forest.

species.name: Crimean Linden
species.intro: Tilia x euchlora is not a tree anyone found in the wild. It is a hybrid raised in cultivation around 1860, small-leaved lime crossed with a Caucasian relative, chosen for glossy dark leaves and a tolerance of compacted, polluted city ground that its parents do not share, which is why it turns up on streets and in parks rather than in forests. Rotterdam's stands on the Parklaan, one of a small planting spree that followed Queen Wilhelmina's 1898 coronation. Manchester's is a cluster in a Didsbury park that the Collins Tree Guide's own author called of national importance, though nobody has measured or dated it in print. Vilnius groups its one with two Amur cork trees as a single 1996 heritage object in the Bernardinai Garden. Heidelberg's stands on an ordinary residential street with no age or description ever recorded, protected since 1986 for reasons the register itself never explains.

species.name: Crows Ash / Australian Teak
species.intro: Flindersia australis is a Queensland rainforest hardwood, milled and sold commercially as Australian teak, named for the navigator Matthew Flinders. All three mapped here carry an honesty gap rather than a measured age. The oldest by claim stands in Brisbane City Botanic Gardens, planted in 1884 to replace an older crows ash felled in 1826 to clear the ground for the settlement's first government garden, no relation between the two. A second, in Newstead Park, is dated only by inference: a television gardening segment judged it older than the 1846 house it stands beside and called that over 160 years, a floor rather than a figure. The third lives worse than either, a memorial tree planted in Toowong in September 1924 inside a sandstone planter box, stunted by its own container ever since, dedicated to a town council abolished thirteen months after the planting.

species.name: Date Palm
species.intro: A date palm belongs to an oasis, not a city square, yet three of them have made themselves at home in European parks and gardens. Lisbon's, in the Ninth of April Garden, is the most disputed: the city calls it the tallest tree in the capital at 38 metres, the national register measured it at 26.7, and nobody has climbed up to settle it. Palermo's stands over a Roman mosaic of Alexander the Great hunting a lion, unearthed by accident under Villa Bonanno and left exactly where it was found. Seville's broke its own species' rule entirely: a date palm is meant to grow as a single trunk, and the one in Parque de Maria Luisa forks into a cluster, which is the only reason the city's own survey of singular trees noticed it at all. Three palms, three very different reasons to have made the list.

species.name: Dawn Redwood
species.intro: Every dawn redwood on this page descends from one valley in central China. The species was known only from imprints in stone and filed under extinct until living trees were found there in the 1940s, and seed collected in 1947 and 1948 went out by post to botanical gardens around the world, which is where these came from. The rediscovery gets dated to 1941 and to 1944 depending on which step is being counted, and both dates turn up in the records behind these trees. They are young, most between sixty and eighty years old, and worth the walk anyway, because a conifer that turns rust orange and drops its needles every winter is an odd thing to meet. Portland's coned in 1952, the first any dawn redwood had done in the Western Hemisphere since the species vanished from it. Eight are mapped, spread from Hobart to Boston.

species.name: Douglas Fir
species.intro: The tallest tree in Portland is 74 metres. The tallest tree in Brussels is 33, and it is the same species. That gap is not about care or soil, it is about home ground: Douglas fir grows wild down the Pacific coast, and the one in Portland's Balch Creek canyon is simply standing where it belongs. Everywhere else it is an import with a hard start date, since seed only left the Pacific Northwest for Europe in 1827. Caserta's register claims about two hundred years for its forty metre specimen, which would put it in the ground the year before that, so read the figure as a round number. Hobart's went into the botanical gardens in 1894, seven years before the Australian colonies became a country. Brussels' grew up beside a racecourse that had two grandstands by 1878.

species.name: Downy Oak
species.intro: Downy oak is the tree Umbrian hillsides are made of, usually a modest, crooked field-edge tree that loses out to better species on good ground. The four the site maps are the exception, all in Umbria and none of them small. Two stand around Assisi: one marking the old gate onto the road to the Eremo delle Carceri, the other in the lower hamlet of Valecchie, added to Italy's national register in July 2026 as the tallest monumental tree recorded in the whole region, thirty metres up. The other two grow 150 metres apart on a lane outside Perugia, within eight centimetres of the same girth, on ground the species shares with truffles: Quercus pubescens is one of central Italy's classic truffle hosts, which is part of why a productive one gets left standing. None of the four carries a documented age; Italy's national register has never recorded one.

species.name: Dragon Tree
species.intro: Nobody can date a dragon tree, and that is the species rather than sloppy record keeping. Dracaena draco lays down no annual rings, so every age here is an estimate and some are wide open: the tree in the Parque Genoves in Cadiz is put anywhere between 100 and 200 years. The name comes from the sap. Cut into the bark and the resin that runs out is dark red, sold across Europe for centuries as dragon's blood, a dye and a medicine. Shape is the other reason to go. An old dragon tree spreads into a low dome of blunt branch tips, and the one at the Quinta Conde dos Arcos in Lisbon is more than twice as wide as it is tall, a crown almost 14 metres across on a tree of 6.2 metres. Six are mapped, three of them in Lisbon and two in Palermo.

species.name: Dutch Elm
species.intro: Dutch elm disease is named for the country that first identified it, which makes every mapped tree of this hybrid a small act of defiance. Amsterdam's Oudemanhuispoort elm has turned a brick-walled courtyard into an advantage, reaching 35 metres because the only direction open to it was up, and a second Amsterdam elm is the last of roughly thirty planted outside Centraal station in 1889, the rest lost to the epidemic decades ago. The Hague's Malieveld elm dates to the 1830s and has now outlived two separate waves of the disease, the second and worse one arriving in the 1970s. In Portland, the Rockey elm survived a 1963 demolition order only because an architect parked his car where the removal crew needed to stand. Each of these is a tree the fungus could have taken and did not.

species.name: English Elm
species.intro: Not one of the three English elms mapped here grows in England. Boston has a pair the Globe calls the oldest English elms in the Western Hemisphere, planted somewhere between 1772 and 1812, and Saint-Gaudens built his memorial to Robert Gould Shaw and the Massachusetts 54th around them, on a vault designed to spare their roots. New York's is the Hangman's Elm on Washington Square, more than 300 years old and possibly 346, with a nickname that no court or newspaper record supports. Portland's was the only elm left standing on the north side of its block after the Columbus Day Storm of 1962 gusted to 116 miles an hour and flattened around 15 billion board feet of Pacific Northwest timber. All three came through a century in which most of their species did not.

species.name: European Ash
species.intro: Ash is the tree Europe is losing right now. A fungus from east Asia, harmless to the ashes it evolved alongside, arrived in Poland and has since worked its way west across the continent, which puts a different weight on the four mapped here. The tallest is in Prague, a 37 metre trunk in the one corner of Strahov Monastery the monks left open to the public, protected since 2007 and among the most massive ashes recorded in the Czech Republic. Gdansk's is older than the rifle factory built around it, roughly 280 years against the works that once turned out 2,500 guns a day. Edinburgh's stands in a park whose house is a roofless shell. Munich's carries no age, no size and no history in the city ordinance, only three words: extremely wide-spreading crown.

species.name: European Beech
species.intro: Almost nothing grows under a beech, and the tree is doing it deliberately. The leaves sit in dense overlapping layers that let very little light through, which is why a beech wood feels like a room rather than a thicket, and why left alone most of northern Europe would return to beech forest within two centuries. So a beech in a city park is often the one tree that would have been there anyway, which is what Nuremberg says of its two. The ones worth crossing town for are beeches given open ground, which keep their lower limbs and bring the crown down in a skirt you have to duck under. Prague's Twin Beech reaches 45 metres on a 1620 battlefield. Haarlem's carries a crowned monogram an exiled king cut into it around 1809. Ten cities hold the thirteen mapped here, every one of them north of the Alps.

species.name: European Larch
species.intro: A larch drops its needles every winter, which is unusual for a conifer and part of why the ones that get noticed tend to stand out. Lithuania's State Protected Areas Service records one in the forest near Degsne at 49 metres, the tallest tree of any kind in the country, grown from a stand planted in 1849. Krakow's grows on a slope that was fenced off as woodland between 1902 and 1909 and kept shut to walkers for roughly half a century before the park finally let people in. Reykjavik's stands in Holavallagardur, the city's oldest cemetery, where conifers generally struggle against Iceland's wind and thin soil badly enough that the national forestry society singled this one out in 2011 for having managed it anyway.

species.name: European Pear
species.intro: Nobody planted these to be looked at. A pear is an orchard tree, grown for fruit and replaced when it stops giving any, which is why four old ones spread across four countries is an odd list to be able to make. The oldest is in The Hague, planted in 1638 in the courtyard of an almshouse for women of unblemished character, and the residents have been turning its hard little juttepeers into jelly for something close to four centuries. Helsinki's is the last survivor of a manor orchard and is reckoned the tallest and oldest pear in Finland. Prague's, at around 190 years, stands where a demolished barracks once held the birthplace of the poet Jan Neruda. Warsaw's carries a name and an 1870 planting date that historians have taken apart piece by piece, and the tree keeps the name regardless.

species.name: European White Elm
species.intro: This is the elm that likes wet feet. Ulmus laevis is a floodplain tree, and Berlin's Great Elm of Treptower Park takes that literally: its roots run straight into the Spree, which foresters credit for a vigour unusual at 250 years. It was added to Germany's national heritage list on 25 September 2025, one of the newest entries on it. The species is uncommon at real size in a European city, so the claims made about these four are worth reading. Munich's register says no older elms are known anywhere in the city, and leaves it at that, because neither of the twin trees in the Englischer Garten carries a measured age. Prague's grows on a scrap of former front garden between Wenceslas Square and the main station. Berlin's other, behind Charlottenburg Palace, gains about six millimetres of girth a year and carries no age at all.

species.name: European Yew
species.intro: No tree in Europe grows older than the yew, and no tree is harder to date: the trunk hollows out with age, taking its own tree rings with it, so the oldest yews keep their exact age a permanent secret. Estimates for the great churchyard yews of Britain and Ireland run from several centuries to several thousand years, and in many cases the tree is provably older than the medieval church beside it, because early Christians built next to yews that were already sacred. Every part of the tree except the red flesh of its berries is poisonous, which kept cattle away and longbows supplied. The yews mapped so far, castle gardens and churchyards included, are listed oldest first.

species.name: Fern-leaved Beech
species.intro: Genoa's city hall has a beech in its courtyard and its leaves are wrong. They come out narrow and deeply slashed, closer to a fern frond than to the broad oval a beech is supposed to carry, which is the whole of the fern-leaved beech and the only reason anyone notices one. None of these three can be very old. The form was not around before about 1804 and cannot be relied on to come true from seed, so every specimen is a cutting off another one. Genoa's stands 21 metres with its crown level with the palace's upper windows, and nobody has published a date for it. Munich has the other two, and registers both of them not for size or age but on the strength of how rarely the form turns up anywhere in the city.

species.name: Field Elm
species.intro: French has a phrase for being kept waiting: attendez-moi sous l'orme, wait for me under the elm. The elm in question stood in front of the Saint-Gervais church in Paris, where debts were repaid on agreed days and judges heard disputes in the shade, and an elm has stood on that spot since the Middle Ages. The one there now was planted in 1935, after the Revolution felled its predecessor, allegedly for cannon carriages; the motif survives in the wrought iron balconies around the square, worked into the metal in the 1730s. Ulmus minor was the species Dutch elm disease hit hardest, which is why the other two matter. Vienna's was planted in 1915 on a green strip down the middle of a street. Trento's is 393 centimetres round and carries no age at all.

species.name: Field Maple
species.intro: Field maple is the tree that fills gaps between hedgerows rather than anchoring a park, which is exactly why the four mapped here stand out from their own species. Prague's, in the Seminary Garden above a pond, carries the group's most precise age, estimated at 160 to 170 years. Graz protects two: one on the wooded Schlossberg hill with no recorded age at all, and one in the Augarten already listed as protection-worthy in a 1956 survey, decades before its formal 1979 designation, giving it a documented floor of at least seventy years. Lisbon's, in Parque Bensaude, has no dated record either. Acer campestre rarely gets a second look; these four earned protection or a place on this map anyway.

species.name: Fig
species.intro: A fig this size stops being a single trunk and becomes a structure. Nago's Hinpun Gajumaru is the clearest case: its aerial roots fused into a mass nearly 12 metres around, wide enough that no one measures a trunk at all, and old enough to have gradually swallowed a pine growing beside it, referenced in Ryukyuan poetry by the 1690s. Rio de Janeiro's fig on Rua Faro became the city's very first landmarked tree in 1980, and only after neighbours physically stood under it to stop a construction crew. Alicante's fig gets a gentler kind of protection: fireproof tarps wrapped around it every June before the plaza around it is set alight for the Fogueres festival, a shield that failed in 2026 and scorched part of its crown. None of the three has ever been keyed to an exact species, so each ships as Ficus sp. rather than a guess.

species.name: Giant Sequoia
species.intro: The heaviest living things on earth reached Europe only in 1853, and the timing shaped everything: Victorian Britain was at peak plant mania, and a tree that could outweigh a blue whale sold itself. Nurserymen shipped seeds by the ton, aristocrats raced to plant avenues of them, and the British even named the species Wellingtonia after the recently dead duke, a name Californians never accepted. Every sequoia outside America is therefore young, barely 170 years at most, yet many already dominate their skylines, because the species grows fast and simply does not stop: in the Sierra Nevada they pass 3,000 years and eighty metres. The sequoias mapped so far are Europe's biggest infants, largest and oldest first.

species.name: Ginkgo
species.intro: The ginkgo has no living relatives. Its family goes back over 200 million years, so far that when the first botanists examined one they were looking at a tree older than flowers; everything else in its lineage is fossil. It nearly vanished too, surviving in Chinese temple grounds until monks and then Dutch traders carried it around the world. It is almost comically hard to kill: six ginkgos stood within two kilometres of the Hiroshima blast and all six leafed the following spring. Cities love it for that same stubbornness, and every November it pays them back, dropping all its golden fan-shaped leaves at once, sometimes in a single day. The ginkgos mapped so far run from Tokyo's shrine giants to the first European imports, oldest first.

species.name: Gray Poplar
species.intro: Gray poplar is a natural cross between white poplar and aspen, and it grows fast enough that a thick trunk is no proof of great age the way it would be on an oak. Warsaw's, on a pavement corner in Mokotow, was surveyed for its national register listing at 21 metres tall and 3.58 metres round, with nobody able to say whether it stood through the 1944 uprising. Sofia's is the oldest tree in the Doctors' Garden, planted in 1892, four years before the garden itself formally opened as one of the city's first botanical collections, and its survival as an ordinary wild-type poplar among later, showier imports is part of what earned it protection. Ferrara's, over 150 years old and 4.44 metres round, grew for most of that time screening a private courtyard at the Palazzo dei Diamanti, one of the Italian Renaissance's most recognisable buildings, until a 2023 restoration opened the garden to visitors. All three are protected by name: Poland's and Italy's national monumental-tree registers, and Sofia's own municipal listing.

species.name: Handkerchief Tree
species.intro: The white handkerchiefs are not flowers. Davidia involucrata makes a small dark flower head of no interest whatever and wraps it in two oversized white bracts, modified leaves that hang below it and turn in any breeze. For roughly ten days to a fortnight in May a mature tree carries hundreds of them at once, which is where handkerchief tree, dove tree and ghost tree all come from, and outside those two weeks it is an ordinary looking thing. Western botany did not know the species existed until the French missionary Armand David documented it in the mountains of central China in 1869, and it stayed rare in cultivation because the seed can sit for two winters before it does anything. Three are mapped, in Copenhagen, Edinburgh and Utrecht, and only Edinburgh's has a date: an accession number that opens 1928.

species.name: Himalayan Cedar
species.intro: Not one of these eighteen trees grows within three thousand kilometres of the mountains it is named after. Cedrus deodara comes from the western Himalaya, from Afghanistan through to Nepal, where deodar means timber of the gods and a tree can pass a thousand years. It reached Europe in 1822 and the continent's park builders took to it at once: Florence's specimen was on the botanical garden's books by 1880, and Bergamo's stands alone in the middle of a lawn with its own lightning conductor, because it is the tallest thing for some distance. The drooping branch tips are the field mark that separates a deodar from the stiffer cedars of Lebanon and the Atlas. Thirteen cities hold them, most of them Italian, and the two registers that measured the one in Rome disagree about its waist by nearly two metres.

species.name: Holm Oak
species.intro: The holm oak is the oak most northern visitors fail to recognise: evergreen, with small dark leathery leaves closer to an olive's than to the lobed oak leaf on every pub sign, holly-like enough that holm is simply the old English word for holly. Around the Mediterranean it is the landscape itself, the dark domed canopy of Spanish dehesas where pigs fatten on its acorns for jamon iberico, and it shrugs off drought, salt wind and poor soil that would kill its deciduous cousins. Planted north of its range it grows slowly into dense, near-black domes that read as older than they are. The holm oaks mapped so far are listed oldest first.

species.name: Honey Locust
species.intro: A wild honey locust is armed. Branched thorns up to fifteen centimetres long grow straight out of the trunk and the older wood, generally read as a defence against browsing animals that no longer exist in North America. Street plantings use thornless varieties, which is part of why the three here look so different from one another. Zaragoza's had three main branches taken out of it at some point and came out the far side as a parasol, a flat horizontal crown on a short trunk. Florence's has never been bred for anything: five and a half metres round, standing alone at a residential junction, and known locally as Spino di Giuda, which people regularly confuse with the pink flowered tree of the same legend. Copenhagen's has been surveyed and remeasured since 1941, twelve metres then and sixteen in 2019.

species.name: Hornbeam
species.intro: Carpinus betulus is Europe's shear-proof hedge tree, planted by the thousand for its density and its patience under a blade, which is why a hornbeam left alone to grow into its full, fluted-trunked shape reads as a surprise. Three stand mapped here, none of them clipped. Aarhus's, in Moesgard's landscape garden, was measured in 2022 at nineteen metres, taller than the species usually reads, its only flaw a little shade thrown by nearby planes. Copenhagen's, in Frederiksberg Have, carries no age or measurement on the Danish national register at all, only a name, Suttetraeet, the pacifier tree, harvested bare every November when local toddlers tie up the dummy they have agreed to give up. Nijmegen's grows a few metres from Krayenhoffpark's giant sequoia, roughly the same age at around 120 years, the only shade in its railway district older than the houses around it.

species.name: Horse Chestnut
species.intro: Every conker in Europe descends from a handful of mountain ravines in northern Greece, Albania and North Macedonia, the only places the horse chestnut still grows wild and where it is now classed as vulnerable. Everywhere else it is a planted tree, and cities planted it hard. Vienna lined its grandest avenue with chestnuts from 1840. Munich's brewers put them over their beer cellars, because the species throws heavy shade from shallow roots that will not force their way into a vault, and the beer garden followed from there. Geneva went further than anyone: since 1818 an official has walked to a designated chestnut each spring, recorded the date its first leaf opens and reported it to the press, which makes one of the longest continuous records of its kind anywhere. Seventeen are mapped, in fifteen cities, and not one of them is anywhere near the wild population.

species.name: Hungarian Oak
species.intro: Quercus frainetto is a large-leaved oak native to the Balkans and southeast Europe, reaching parks and streets further north only because someone planted it there on purpose. Three mapped here carry very different reasons why. Glasgow's grew from a single afternoon in April 1918: days after some British women won the vote, suffrage campaigner Louisa Lumsden planted this oak in Kelvingrove Park on behalf of four rival suffrage groups that agreed, for once, to plant a tree together rather than argue tactics. It is now Scotland's Tree of the Year, still recovering the crown Storm Ophelia tore off in 2017. The Hague's group of three, dated to around 1900, are civic planting from the same continental-collecting era. Warsaw's stands at the corner where Janusz Korczak ran his orphanage until German soldiers marched him and his children to Treblinka in 1942; the tree beside it is named for him.

species.name: Indian Banyan
species.intro: An Indian banyan does not grow a single trunk so much as recruit one. Aerial roots drop from its limbs, thicken into props where they reach the ground, and fuse with their neighbours into a mass that a tape measure reads as one continuous trunk, which is why the girth can run to absurd lengths without the tree being especially old. Brisbane's, planted in the City Botanic Gardens during Walter Hill's curatorship in the 1870s, measures 49 metres round by two independent counts, the National Trust's and the State Library of Queensland's, and is rated the finest example of the species in Australia. Singapore's, in Tiong Bahru Park, wins on speed rather than size: NParks' own register says it was planted after the park opened in 1967, so it reached 22.8 metres of girth in under sixty years, wider than trees centuries older. Hilo has two, both protected under Hawaii's 1975 tree law: one in Kalakaua Park, 18.6 metres round, planted in 1882 by either a sheriff or a king depending which account is believed; the other left unmeasured entirely, a blank line on the state register, growing quietly along the trail past Rainbow Falls. None of the four can be aged from its girth, because the number describes a colony's width, not a stem's.

species.name: Indian Laurel Fig
species.intro: Hong Kong keeps a category of tree that almost nowhere else bothers with. A stone wall tree grows straight out of a masonry retaining wall, roots threaded down through the joints, and the department responsible for several of them is not the one that runs the parks but the one that looks after government masonry. Twenty-seven of them line three walls on Forbes Street, and when engineers planned to extend the MTR through Kennedy Town the station was rerouted rather than the wall removed. The species is common enough that the city plants it by the thousand and almost never lets one grow old. The exception is the King Banyan in Kowloon Park, put at four hundred years and still the largest urban tree in the city after a 2007 typhoon took a third of its trunk. Eight mapped, in Hong Kong, Malaga and Seville.

species.name: Japanese Black Pine
species.intro: Pinus thunbergii is the pine of the Japanese coast, tough enough for salt spray and heavy snow, and gardeners have spent centuries training it into shapes weather alone never would. Kanazawa strings ropes from a pole above its Karasaki pine every November so wet snow cannot break the limbs, the yukitsuri rigging that has become the picture of the city in winter; nearby, a Maeda lord is said to have raised another pine on a mound of earth and stripped the soil away, leaving forty-odd roots standing clear of the ground. Tokyo's grows in a garden the bay still floods daily on purpose, planted around 1709 and spent three centuries spreading rather than climbing. Nara's is simply the fattest survivor of a planting habit with no purpose but looking right: three and a half metres round, roughly two hundred and fifty years old. Five mapped so far, across four cities.

species.name: Japanese Cedar
species.intro: A picture scroll donated to Kasuga Taisha in 1309 shows this shrine's great cedar as a sapling. Seven centuries on it is roughly eight metres round and twenty five tall, and it is the same organism, which makes it one of very few ancient trees anywhere that can be checked against its own portrait as a young plant. A second tree took root in its base and grew toward the neighbouring hall, and rather than cut it back somebody cut a hole in the roof; the hole is still there. Fukuoka's cedar at Kashii Shrine is traditionally dated at about 1,800 years, from a legend that Empress Jingu pushed a branch from her armour into the ground here. Kyoto's stands in the old imperial timber forest and layers under heavy snow, rooting where the trunk is pinned down.

species.name: Japanese Chinquapin
species.intro: Sudajii, the Japanese chinquapin, was the dominant tree of the evergreen broadleaf forest that once covered lowland western Japan, before it was cleared for rice, timber and capital cities, so a mature one standing inside a city today is a leftover of the landscape the city replaced. Kyoto's grows at the Omiya gate of Kyoto Gyoen, on ground that outlasted the forest around it. Kanazawa's pair flank the entrance of the old Ishikawa prefectural office, made a National Natural Monument in 1943, built low and broad rather than tall. Tokyo's, roughly four hundred years old and eight metres round, grows on the former Hosokawa estate where Oishi Kuranosuke is said to have been held after the Ako Incident of 1701.

species.name: Japanese Maple
species.intro: Japanese maples are usually shrubs, small enough to see over, so a specimen that clears a metre round and earns a place on an official monumental-tree register is genuinely unusual. The Netherlands has two on this site: one in Arnhem's Park Angerenstein, dated to the 1920s and protected on dendrological grounds alone, nothing historical attached, the tree itself being the whole reason; and one in Maastricht's Waldeckpark, whose register band of 1910 to 1920 sits oddly early against the park's own 1921 layout, a discrepancy nobody has resolved. Japan's own entry needs no register to prove itself: a temple maple in Iwaki whose age nobody will state, but whose autumn colour the city government tracks and publishes year by year, which is a different, more useful kind of record than an age nobody can verify.

species.name: Japanese Nutmeg-yew
species.intro: Torreya nucifera, called kaya in Japan, is a slow evergreen conifer that looks the same in February as in August, which is part of why its oldest specimens went unnoticed for centuries. Three of the four mapped here are named, without much argument, as Japan's three great kaya: one in Maebashi at 8.1 metres round, one in Saitama traditionally dated to the 1030s, one on private farmland near Hamamatsu that visitors view from the road. The fourth, at Nagoya Castle, carries a stranger claim to fame: the first Owari lord ate its nuts before marching on Osaka in 1615, in the campaign that finished the Toyotomi and secured Tokugawa rule for two and a half centuries, and his successors kept eating them every New Year after. None of the four gives up its age easily; growth rings, girth surveys and shrine tradition all disagree, sometimes by centuries.

species.name: Japanese Pagoda Tree
species.intro: This tree flowers cream in August, when almost nothing else in a European city is doing anything at all, and that habit is most of the reason it was ever planted. Despite the name it is Chinese rather than Japanese, brought into European gardens in the eighteenth century and set out in squares and courtyards where lunch happens outdoors. Vienna, Munich and the City of London each protect one. The oldest here is not European: the pagoda tree in the courtyard of Jogyesa in Seoul is put at 400 to 450 years, older than the temple hall beside it, and every Buddha's Birthday its crown disappears under thousands of paper lanterns. Kew's, planted in 1762, is one of the five veterans the garden's first curator nicknamed the Old Lions. Eleven cities so far, twelve trees.

species.name: Japanese White Pine
species.intro: All three of these pines have been shaped by hand for six centuries or more, and all three are in Kyoto. The one beside the pond at Kinkaku-ji was a bonsai in a pot belonging to Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, the shogun who built the Golden Pavilion; after his death in 1408 it was planted out and clipped, generation after generation, into a sailing ship with its bow pointed west toward the Pure Land. Yoshimine-dera's grows almost flat instead of upward, named the playing dragon in 1857 and once fifty metres end to end, until bark beetles in 1994 cost it fifteen. Hosen-in's is the subject of a picture frame garden: you sit on a red felt cushion in a wooden hall and look at it through a doorway. That tree is trained to echo Mount Mikami, a cone shaped peak southeast of the city.

species.name: Japanese Wisteria
species.intro: Japanese wisteria is usually a garden plant, trained onto a frame and pruned into the tunnels and canopies most visitors picture. The vines mapped here mostly are not. At Yama-jinja, in the shadow of Mount Fuji, two vines seeded themselves and climbed unassisted, one of only eight climbing plants in Japan with National Natural Monument status, granted in 1928; a typhoon later forced the older vine onto a support frame it never asked for. Ichinohe's vine, several hundred years old by local account, is untrained too. Only Tokyo's Kameido Tenjin wisteria followed the cultivated tradition, planted after the shrine's founding in 1663 because the marshy ground suited the species, and it has a claim stranger than its age: art historians trace a line from Hiroshige's 1856 print of it, arched drum bridge and all, to the wisteria Monet later planted at Giverny.

species.name: Judas Tree
species.intro: The flowers come straight out of the bark. Cercis siliquastrum is cauliflorous, so in spring, before a single leaf opens, rosy purple blossom breaks directly from the trunk and the old wood, and the tree looks briefly upholstered rather than in bloom. The name is old and unkind, from the tradition that Judas hanged himself from one, though it may be nothing more than a garbled Judaea. This is a small tree that goes sideways: the one on Placa Joanic in Barcelona is five metres tall under a crown ten metres across. Cordoba's stands at the gate of the San Rafael cemetery and is the largest of its species in the province. Vienna's, in the grounds of the old general hospital, is well over a century old and may be eighteenth century. The fourth is at the Fer a Cheval in Toulouse. Go in spring, before the leaves.

species.name: Kapok
species.intro: Kapok is a rainforest giant, native to tropical lowland forest where it pushes its crown above the canopy on wide buttress roots, which makes every one we map a tree standing somewhere unlikely. Singapore's, at the foot of Mount Faber, has an 11.55 metre girth, among the largest trunks on the city's entire heritage register. Honolulu's was planted around 1851 by the German physician William Hillebrand on what was then his own homestead, and is now the oldest tree in the botanical garden later built around it. Lima's grows in a green strip in San Isidro, a rainforest species holding on in a coastal desert city whose weather is mostly grey sea fog.

species.name: Katsura
species.intro: Katsura grows wild in the old forests of Japan, and the trees mapped here show how far its reputation travels from there. On Sapporo's Maruyama hill, inside a national natural monument forest, one katsura reaches enormous size on the shaded north slope; at the hot spring in Koganeyu, a katsura became a god, worshipped as Fudo Myoo standing in tree form, with a torii and a straw rope in front of it. The Boston pair carries the species further still: grown from seed William S. Clark, the American college president who helped found Hokkaido University, collected in 1876 and sent to his friend Charles Sprague Sargent, the Arnold Arboretum's first director, arriving in 1878. A tree tied to fire and water in Japanese folklore now shades a meadow in Jamaica Plain because two men once traded seed packets across an ocean. Three mapped so far, in two countries.

species.name: Kauri
species.intro: A kauri does not look like other big trees, because it throws away the parts that would make it look like one. It sheds its lower branches as it grows and flakes off its lower bark in plates, which keeps climbers and epiphytes off the trunk, so what you walk up to is a bare grey column with the crown a long way overhead. Tane Mahuta in the Waipoua Forest is 45 metres tall and most of that is column. Te Matua Ngahere, twenty minutes away in the same forest, went the other way: shorter, squatter, and thicker round than anything else standing in New Zealand. Both are protected from their visitors as much as for them, because a soil-borne disease called kauri dieback travels on the mud in a shoe tread, which is why there are cleaning stations at both tracks and why a third famous tree in that forest is currently closed off entirely. The third one mapped here is a long way from home: a mature kauri on the Plaza de Panama in San Diego, a species almost nobody grows in southern California, standing beside a museum with almost nothing written down about it.

species.name: Kentucky Coffeetree
species.intro: The genus this tree belongs to has exactly two species in the world, this one and a Chinese cousin, and it survives mostly because people kept planting it. The Kentucky coffeetree takes its English name from settlers who roasted and ground its seeds as a coffee substitute, a recipe not worth reviving since the raw seeds and pods are toxic. It is dioecious, male and female flowers on separate trees, so only a female standing near a male sets the thick leathery pods. What gives it away in any season is timing: it leafs out later than almost anything else nearby, often not before late May, then drops early and spends the rest of the year as a set of bare, blunt grey branches so stark that the Dutch call it the dead men's bones tree and the French call it chicot, stump, because passersby assume it has died. The three this site maps show the range: a young register specimen in Brussels' Parc d'Egmont, a 130-year-old survivor in Bordeaux's Parc Bordelais fenced and pruned around cavities in its trunk, and a tree planted near Ottawa's Queen Elizabeth Driveway at the turn of the twentieth century, this far north stubbornly out of range.

species.name: Lacebark Pine
species.intro: Most pines are planted for their needles or their shape. This one is planted for its bark, which sheds in irregular plates of olive, grey-green and chalk white until an old trunk looks close to ivory, a trait so distinctive the species barely needs its Latin name to identify it. Pinus bungeana is native to China, and every specimen mapped here arrived somewhere else as a deliberate transplant. Lyon's, in the Parc de la Tête d'Or arboretum, was probably planted in 1856 and is known locally as the Pin de Napoléon. Pittsburgh's stands in Mellon Park, named to the city's own official Remarkable Trees list in 2023 for its bark alone, with no age on record. Seoul's, beside the Constitutional Court in Jae-dong, carries a six-century legend that a Ming dynasty envoy brought it as a gift, unproven but attached to the tree for generations. Three cities so far.

species.name: Large-leaved Lime
species.intro: A lime has marked the exact spot where three Brussels communes meet since at least 1777, and that is the sort of job this species keeps getting: boundary post, landmark, the tree a place organises itself around. Munich protects one of these in law for its bizarre growth, which is an unusual reason to make a tree a natural monument. Prague has one a president refused to lose, Tomas Garrigue Masaryk having had a castle terrace built around it. Telling a large-leaved lime from a small-leaved one is harder than it sounds, and under Nuremberg's 400 year old tree the sign and the botanists who have looked at its leaves still disagree. Seven are mapped across six cities, among them an Antwerp linden protected since 2010 for precisely where it stands rather than for anything rare about the tree itself.

species.name: Lime
species.intro: These are the limes nobody has narrowed to a single species, planted or grown before anyone thought to record which Tilia they were, which is common enough with a genus this widely hybridised that the honest label is simply Tilia sp. Amsterdam's Wilhelminalinde went into the ground on the Kalverstraat to mark Queen Wilhelmina's 1898 coronation and is a tidy, dateable 128 years old. Nuremberg's gnarled lime at the Hallerwiese has taken lightning and storm damage across some three and a half centuries and is still putting on growth, damaged and healthy in the same trunk. Frankfurt's eight-stemmed linden in Grüneburgpark is not one tree that happened to fork; it is a deliberate bundle planting, several saplings set into one hole so they would fuse into a single crown, rare enough to be a protected natural monument in its own right.

species.name: Lombardy Poplar
species.intro: Lombardy poplar is the columnar form of black poplar, propagated only from cuttings of a single line, so every one traces back to the same origin tree and none of them set seed. It is also famously short-lived: usually rotten by fifty, gone by seventy, planted by the million and protected almost nowhere. The three mapped here are the exceptions. Amsterdam's stands as a living pilaster in the Rijksmuseum's garden of salvaged doorways, planted within a few decades of the museum's 1885 opening. Seattle's grew up beside the temporary Fine Arts Palace built for the 1909 Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition and has now outlasted the building it was planted to frame. Portland's, out on the eastern edge of the city, carries the widest trunk on the entire heritage tree register at 9.75 metres round, an absurd measurement for a tree built to be thin.

species.name: London Plane
species.intro: The London plane is a tree that a city adopted and then named after itself. It is a hybrid, a cross between the American sycamore and the Oriental plane that appeared in Europe in the 1600s and turned out to be almost indestructible in a dirty city: it shrugs off soot, tolerates brutal pruning, and sheds its bark in patches to slough off pollution. That made it the default street tree of industrial London, and from there of Paris, Amsterdam and half the capitals of Europe. The oldest specimens are now three centuries old and enormous, and because the tree was planted everywhere, the remarkable ones hide in plain sight: a churchyard in the City of London, a Mayfair square, a riverside suburb. These are the London planes mapped on the site so far, oldest first.

species.name: Maple
species.intro: These are the maples nobody has narrowed to species, recorded at genus level because the field evidence was never gathered or settled. Badhoevedorp's roadside maple grows in a private front garden, and the register disagrees with itself: one entry bands its planting to 1910-1920, another note says 1895, which would put the tree on the dike before the house beside it was built. Utrecht holds two more, both filed by their neighbours rather than their own names. One stands south of a memorial beech in Zonnenburg, a bastion park Jan David Zocher jr laid out in 1835, sycamore or Norway maple depending on how its winged seeds hang. The other pair, by the Andrea monument in Wilhelminapark, flowers red in February before a single leaf opens, most likely silver maples by their pale, deeply cut foliage, though nobody has confirmed it from a leaf underside yet.

species.name: Mastic Tree
species.intro: Pistacia lentiscus spends most of its life as a shrub, a low, dense presence across Mediterranean scrubland that most walkers step past without a glance. Left standing for long enough, on the right ground, it does something else: pushes up a real trunk and takes on the shape and size of a proper tree, which is exactly why the specimens mapped here were singled out. The species is best known commercially for mastic resin, tapped for millennia from trees on the Greek island of Chios and used in everything from chewing gum to varnish. One specimen here, in Istanbul, is put at roughly 500 years old, a genuine outlier for a plant almost nobody lets live that long. Three mapped, in Barcelona, Istanbul and Palma de Mallorca.

species.name: Mediterranean Cypress
species.intro: The Mediterranean cypress is the most recognisable punctuation mark in landscape: a dark green exclamation point that Van Gogh painted obsessively and that Greeks, Romans and Persians planted at graves for three thousand years before him. The mourning association is practical as much as poetic, because the tree is close to immortal by garden standards, evergreen, drought-proof and content on thin stony soil, exactly the qualities you want from something meant to outlast grief. Its species name sempervirens simply means always alive. Individual cypresses in Iran are credibly claimed at four thousand years. The cypresses mapped so far stand in cemeteries, monastery courtyards and old gardens, oldest first.

species.name: Mediterranean Hackberry
species.intro: Italians call this tree spaccasassi, the stone splitter, because its roots get into paving and open it, and cities across southern Europe plant it in their squares regardless, because little else gives that much shade on that little water. Celtis australis is deep rooted, drought hardy and indifferent to heat, with a smooth grey trunk closer to a beech than an oak and small dark berries that taste faintly of dates. Mostly it is treated as background, which is why the exceptions stand out. Istanbul protects one by name. Munich registers a group of eight as an extremely rare species, five hundred kilometres north of where the tree grows wild. And a hackberry in Zaragoza came third in Spain's national tree of the year vote in December 2025, put forward by five neighbourhood associations rather than the city. Sixteen are mapped, in thirteen cities, most of them Italian or Spanish.

species.name: Mexican Cypress
species.intro: A Mexican tree carries the name lusitanica, meaning Portuguese, and the tree responsible for the mistake is still standing. When Philip Miller described the species in 1768 he was working from cypresses growing at Bucaco, where Carmelite monks had planted them, and named it for where he found it rather than where it came from. The Cedro de Sao Jose, about 380 years old, is one of those trees, and a second stands further along the Via Sacra beside the station marking Christ's first fall. Portugal has called the species cedro-do-Bucaco ever since, which compounds the error, since it is a cypress and no kind of cedar. Lisbon's first legally protected tree, presiding over the Praca do Principe Real, goes by that name too. The oldest of the four is in Granada at roughly 440 years, named for San Juan de la Cruz.

species.name: Mexican Fan Palm
species.intro: The building these palms were planted for was demolished in 1951 and the palms are still standing: seven Mexican fan palms in a line at the Palacio de Cristal in Porto, roughly 160 years old, outliving the glass hall they were meant to frame. That is the pattern with this species in Europe, which arrives as instant architecture and then outlasts it. Granada's four went up over the Plaza de Gracia in 1923, the year the palace behind them was finished. Palermo's line an avenue in the Villa Giulia, which opened in 1778 and is generally counted as Italy's first public garden. Valencia has two from the early twentieth century, one of them the result of a gardener's error that left it standing where it should not have been, taller and thinner than every palm around it.

species.name: Monterey Cypress
species.intro: In the wild this tree grows on two headlands near Monterey in California and nowhere else on earth, together covering less than a square kilometre. Give it a mild wet winter anywhere and it grows fast and enormous, which is how it reached Italian and Portuguese gardens within a few decades of being described. Trieste's stands at Miramare, put in after 1856 when Archduke Maximilian laid out a park around his castle on the sea, and is about 170 years old. Lucca's grows on the San Regolo bastion, part of the ring of Renaissance walls the city turned into a promenade.
