Florence has one in the Giardino Simone Weil and Lisbon one in the Parque do Caramao da Ajuda, roughly 95 years old. Four trees in four cities, all of them exiles from a coastline you could walk in an afternoon.

species.name: Montezuma Cypress
species.intro: This is the species that holds the fattest trunk on earth, the Arbol del Tule in Oaxaca, and the four mapped here are working in the same direction if nowhere near the same scale. Florence's is seven metres around and was hit by lightning barely a decade ago. Lisbon's, in the Jardim da Parada, is six and a half metres around and the biggest thing in a garden that fills an entire city block. Taxodium mucronatum is Mexico's national tree, the ahuehuete, planted at springs by the Aztecs, and Naples has nicknamed its own the Tree of Thule after the giant in Oaxaca. Madrid's, in the Retiro's parterre, comes with two origin stories that cannot both be true and estimates running from 200 years to 390. In a mild winter it keeps enough of its needles never to look properly bare.

species.name: Moreton Bay Fig
species.intro: A Moreton Bay fig announces itself at ground level first: buttress roots the height of a person come snaking across the earth like walls, and the trunk they support looks less grown than poured. In its native eastern Australia the species often starts life as a strangler high in another tree, sends roots down, and eventually stands on its own; planted in the mild coastal cities of Europe and beyond in the 19th century, it skipped the strangling and went straight to the monumental, single trees shading entire plazas within a human lifetime. It needs frost-free air, which is why every great specimen marks a mild microclimate. The Moreton Bay figs mapped so far are listed largest and oldest first.

species.name: Narrow-Leaved Ash
species.intro: Fraxinus angustifolia is the ash of southern Europe, a riverside species that follows watercourses through country too dry for its northern cousin, and for centuries it was pollarded for fodder and tool handles rather than left to grow free. That habit shapes the three mapped here differently. Girona's, at L'Aulet in Vidreres, carries a 5.90 metre trunk built from decades of repeated cutting, a short massive base under a crown that is all regrowth. Barcelona's grew the opposite way, straight up a Montjuic quarry pit whose damp, sheltered air let it reach 29 metres, the tallest of its species recorded anywhere in Catalonia. Leiden's stands furthest from home, planted in a Dutch botanical garden around 1818 and grafted, the swelling from that graft still visible after two centuries. Ash dieback is moving through Europe regardless of species, which makes a healthy veteran worth finding while it stands.

species.name: Norfolk Island Hibiscus
species.intro: Lagunaria patersonii comes from one small island in the Tasman Sea, Norfolk Island, a native range of about thirty-five square kilometres that makes almost anywhere else it grows a transplant by definition. Coastal cities plant it for a practical reason: it tolerates salt wind and poor soil better than most ornamental trees, and it flowers in summer in pale pink cups that pass for a small hibiscus. The seed pods carry the species' other reputation, packed with fine hairs that itch for hours if opened carelessly, which is why English speakers call it the itchy bomb tree. Three mapped, in Setubal, Barcelona and Palma de Mallorca.

species.name: Norfolk Island Pine
species.intro: The entire species comes from one Pacific island eight kilometres long, and it now stands over port cities from Hobart to the Atlantic coast of Portugal. Araucaria heterophylla grows in regular tiers, a candelabra of horizontal branches on a dead straight stem, which is why it reads as a tree drawn by a child and why nineteenth century gardeners could not resist it. Height is usually the point. The Malaga specimen, around 200 years old, is the tallest in its province; Barcelona's clears 27 metres above one of the most densely built neighbourhoods in Europe; Sintra's is the tallest tree at Monserrate. Setubal has six of them at 26 metres, standing in a ring around one old circular stone tank with a fountain in the middle. Hobart's is the one nearest home, and a local nurseryman asked in 2025 to name his favourite tree in the city picked it.

species.name: Northern Red Oak
species.intro: Brussels Environment's own walking route through the Parc d'Egmont gives up on describing its red oak and tells you to come back in autumn instead. That is the whole reason a North American tree ended up on European streets: nothing native turns that colour. Five of the six mapped here are European plantings and only one is at home, growing on the Spicebush Trail in a 50 acre patch of old forest inside the New York Botanical Garden. Milan has two, one beside the site of one of the city's six historic gates and one on a horse racing track that stopped racing a century ago and became a school. Prague's stands on the island where the city's archers used to practise. The Baarn oak, roughly 175 years old, wears a ring carrying words the municipality asked its residents to write in 2021.

species.name: Norway Maple
species.intro: Norway maple is one of the most planted street trees in Europe, valued for tolerating road salt, compacted soil and bad air, and just as routinely cut back once it outgrows its spot. The three mapped here are what a city decided to keep instead. One stands on a two-metre-thick fortress bastion in Den Bosch, on parkland made after the earthwork's old defensive windmill came down and the ramparts stopped being military. Munich protects two more under a 2021 natural monument ordinance built for the exception rather than the rule: one on Mondstrasse is named a singular tree that defines its square, the other on Herrnstrasse survives simply for being rare at its size among five storeys of inner-city courtyards. Snap a leaf stalk on either and it bleeds white sap, the surest way to tell a Norway maple from the sycamore maple it is otherwise mistaken for.

species.name: Norway Spruce
species.intro: Norway spruce belongs to mountain forests, the slopes of the Balkans and Scandinavia, not to city parks, so every spruce on this site got there by somebody's deliberate choice. Sofia's tallest, in Borisova Garden, was planted in 1885 by the writer Ivan Vazov and has since outgrown the marble bust raised to him decades later. Near Rothenburg, two spruces stand over a small waterfall in the Vorbachtal, registered by Bavaria as one natural monument rather than two, their exact age unrecorded. In Reykjavik, a spruce on the island of Elliðaárhólmi was named Iceland's Tree of the Year in 2019, twelve metres tall and barely older than most of the visitors who come to see it, proof that a country with almost no native forest left can still grow something worth naming.

species.name: Oak
species.intro: Twelve oaks on this map carry only their genus, Quercus, because nobody has yet taken a leaf close enough to say which species each one is. That gap does not make them less worth the walk. Belfast's Belvoir Oak got down to six acorns one winter, all its crown could still manage, and is still standing. Ypres's Christusboom has been cut to nothing by two wars and grown back from the stump both times. Austin's Auction Oaks shaded the 1839 sale of town lots before the city existed, and the Seiders Oaks nearby saved a settler's life in a fight with mounted raiders three years later. Hainich's Betteleiche is hollow because medieval friars are said to have carved it out to keep alms dry. If you can tell a pedunculate from a sessile oak at a glance, tell us.

species.name: Ohatsuki Ginkgo
species.intro: Most ginkgos hang their seeds on a stalk, apart from the branch. This mutation grows them straight out of the leaf blade itself, first described to Japanese science in July 1891 from a specimen in Minobu, Yamanashi. Only seven trees of the kind hold National Natural Monument status, and an unexplained three of them stand within two kilometres of each other in that one district: one toppled by Typhoon Trami in 2018 and still fruiting from its fallen trunk, another the sole male of the seven, its single fertile branch discovered only in 2011 after decades of nothing, and a third that local legend has the monk Nichiren planting himself in 1282. None has a documented planting date; all three ages here stay broad estimates rather than measurements.

species.name: Olive
species.intro: No tree has been in continuous employment longer than the olive. Humans have cultivated it for at least six thousand years, and individual trees stay on the payroll for a thousand or more, still setting fruit on trunks so twisted and split they look geological rather than botanical. That endurance is built in: an olive regrows from its base after fire, frost or felling, so the gnarled base can be many centuries older than every branch above it. The ancient world treated the tree accordingly, as the literal embodiment of peace, victory and civic pride; Athens named itself over one. The olives mapped so far, some relocated into city squares, some in their original groves, are listed oldest first.

species.name: Ombu
species.intro: None of this is wood. Phytolacca dioica is a giant herb that behaves like a tree, a soft stemmed relative of spinach whose swollen base is water storing tissue you could dent with a thumbnail, laid down for the dry seasons of the Argentine pampas it comes from. It grows fast, yields no timber worth the name, and cannot be aged by counting rings, which is why the one in Cadiz is undated and honestly so. What it does instead is get very wide. Two in a single Lisbon garden came out at 10.45 and 10.4 metres around, and the one at Largo do Limoeiro is described as reaching some seventeen metres at the base, wider than the house fronts on the street. Seville's is credited to seed that Christopher Columbus's son brought back around 1529. Seven are mapped, and three of them stand in Lisbon.

species.name: Oriental Plane
species.intro: Before the London plane existed, its eastern parent was already the most storied shade tree in the world. Hippocrates is said to have taught medicine under an Oriental plane on Kos, Herodotus tells of a Persian king who halted an entire army to decorate one, and across Greece, Turkey and the Balkans the village square and the plane above it grew up as a single institution. The species hollows as it ages without weakening much, which lets individual trees pass five hundred years while whole communities hold meetings, weddings and cafes inside and beneath them. The Oriental planes mapped so far include spring-side giants that predate the towns around them, oldest first.

species.name: Osage Orange
species.intro: Every autumn these trees drop green spheres the size of a grapefruit that nothing alive wants to eat. The fruit of Maclura pomifera looks like a brain, weighs a kilo or more and seems to have been built for animals that vanished from North America thousands of years ago. The tree takes its name from the Osage nation, who made bows from the wood, which is dense and springy and was traded far beyond their own territory. American farmers then found a second use: planted close and cut back, osage orange grows into a thorn hedge nothing can push through, and thousands of miles of it went in through the 1850s until barbed wire made it pointless. All four here are curiosities in European parks, two in Barcelona and one each in Lyon and Toulouse. Stand under one in November and watch your head.

species.name: Pecan
species.intro: A pecan is an odd thing to find towering over a European garden, and yet two of the tallest trees mapped here are exactly that: 38 metres in Bordeaux's Jardin Public, 37 in the Real Alcazar of Seville, both outgrowing every native Mediterranean species planted around them. The species belongs to the river bottoms of Texas and the lower Mississippi, and Dallas keeps two working examples of that native range: a pecan that stood watching the Trinity River crossing before the first bridge went up in 1855, and a disputed elder in Moore Park whose 472 centimetres of girth make it the thickest tree of its kind the city has measured. Planted for nuts as often as for looks, and left standing long after anyone was counting the harvest, a mapped pecan tends to be the tallest thing nobody expected in the garden.

species.name: Pedunculate Oak
species.intro: Foresters used to say an oak spends three hundred years growing, three hundred resting, and three hundred slowly dying. The pedunculate oak, Quercus robur, is the tree that adage was built on: the classic broad English oak of parkland and legend, though it grows just as happily in Amsterdam or Berlin. Its trick for extreme age is to hollow out. As the heartwood rots away the tree keeps only its living outer sleeve, which lightens the load and can extend its life past a thousand years. That is why the oldest oaks are the fattest and most gnarled, not the tallest. Kings prized them enough to wall entire parks around them, and their timber built the navies and cathedrals of northern Europe. These are the ancient oaks mapped on the site so far, oldest first.

species.name: Pin Oak
species.intro:
Pin oak is a North American swamp species, native to wet bottomland from the Great Lakes down through the Mississippi valley, that reached European gardens at the start of the nineteenth century and became a Dutch park favourite decades later. Three are mapped so far: an 1840s planting in Haarlem's Frederikspark, one from the 1860s in Apeldoorn's Oranjepark, and a 1910s specimen in Sittard's Stadspark.

It is easy to place once you have seen one. The lower branches sweep down toward the grass while the upper ones reach up, and the leaves are cut into narrow, bristle-tipped lobes far sharper than any native oak's. The name comes from the small pin-like stubs of dead branchlets along the trunk, not the leaves. All three hold their scarlet October colour and their dead leaves well into winter, so a pin oak is often the last oak in a park still dressed.

species.name: Plane
species.intro: Three planes on this map carry only their genus, Platanus, because whichever register or record named them stopped at that. The Hague's Plane of Park Hoekenburg grows over Forum Hadriani, a Roman port town whose excavation once turned up an oak post felled in the year 212, read straight off its rings. Hoorn's Plane of Number 37 has the opposite problem: an exact planting date, 1871, at the waterside of the Oosterpoortsgracht, but no species beyond plane. Bratislava's Plane of Kysucká Street stands where nobody planted it for show, on the road up to Zelezna studnicka, protected tree number 231, measured at 6.11 metres round in 2012. Planes hybridise readily and the parents can be hard to call from bark and leaf alone, which is likely why all three were left at genus. If you can tell an Oriental plane from a London plane on sight, tell us.

species.name: Pohutukawa
species.intro: New Zealand's Christmas tree does its flowering here in early summer. Metrosideros excelsa covers itself in scarlet brushes at the height of the southern summer, which in Cadiz, Lisbon, Porto and Sintra falls half a year off its native schedule and a hemisphere from home. At home it grows on sea cliffs, gripping rock with aerial roots, which is close to what the Atlantic edge of Iberia offers it. The Monserrate tree in Sintra is the oldest of the five, though nobody will pin it closer than somewhere between 175 and 275 years. Porto's pair on the grass at Passeio Alegre stand eleven metres apart and are barely taller than a house. Lisbon's two, in the Jardim da Parada, are ten metres apart and protected as separate trees. Five are mapped, four in Portugal and one in Cadiz.

species.name: Poplar
species.intro: Poplars grow fast and die young, which is exactly why the three mapped here stand out: each has outlasted the ordinary run for the genus by decades. None of them is famous for its age. Ofunato's Dokonjo Poplar took the 2011 tsunami half underwater and kept standing, and the city built a memorial plaza around it. Biei's Ken and Mary Tree was just a farm boundary marker until a 1972 car commercial made it one of the most photographed trees in Hokkaido. Arnhem's Wagnerlaan Poplar has an official monument listing and nothing else, not even a settled species. That last gap runs through all three: the sources checked cannot say which poplar any of them is, only that each is a Populus. If you know one on sight, the page says so and asks.

species.name: Queensland Kauri
species.intro: Queensland kauri grows wild only in a strip of eastern Australia, but the species travelled well: every kauri mapped so far stands somewhere else entirely. Sydney's, in the Royal Botanic Garden's Palm Grove, grew from a seed picked on New Year's Day 1849 by the garden's first director and is the type specimen every other Sydney kauri gets measured against, still ahead of its nearest rival after more than 170 years. Hobart's, in the Royal Tasmanian Botanical Gardens, reaches 39 metres and is rare enough to carry four separate significance ratings on the city's tree register, aesthetic, dimensions, age and rarity, where most trees earn one or two. Los Angeles has the oldest and largest kauri in the United States, and it needs no ticket or gate: it stands on an open hillside above Dodger Stadium's parking lots, in the Chavez Ravine Arboretum planted in 1893. Kauris are slow and can run past 300 years, so none of these three, barely two centuries old at most, has finished growing.

species.name: Rain Tree
species.intro: The rain tree gets its name from what it does at the end of the day: the leaflets fold shut at dusk and again when a storm is coming, so the rain falls straight through a canopy that looked solid an hour earlier. In Hawaii nobody calls it that. There it is the monkeypod, and it only arrived around 1847, which is why the Gulick-Rowell tree in Waimea cannot be the 200 years old that local tradition insists on, however good the story about the Indian prince is. Kauai's other one was put in by the shopkeeper whose store it still shades. Oahu's is on Japanese television most weeks as Hitachi's emblem, and almost nobody watching knows it stands in Honolulu. Singapore's spreads over a public stairway out of Fort Canning Park, so everyone taking those steps walks under it whether they look up or not.

species.name: Red Horse Chestnut
species.intro: The red horse chestnut is a cross bred deliberately, joining the white-flowered chestnut of every European avenue with a red-flowered American buckeye, first recorded in Germany around 1820. The result flowers pink in May instead of white, sets almost no spiny conkers, and shrugs off the leaf miner moth that browns out its white parent by late summer. It was planted for gardens, not found in the wild, which shows in where these three stand: a former hospital courtyard in Leeuwarden whose tree survived 1990s redevelopment with crown anchors and a trunk wound to show for it, a public square in Amstelveen with no history recorded at all, and the lawn of a 1748 house in the Bronx, where family tradition says a Van Cortlandt planted it themselves. Three trees, three very different kinds of care.

species.name: River Red Gum
species.intro: Seville and the province of Valencia each have a record holder for height, and both are the same Australian tree, growing thousands of kilometres from where it belongs. Eucalyptus camaldulensis follows the seasonal rivers of inland Australia across almost the whole continent, surviving drought by dropping whole limbs and resprouting from the base, which is a habit that makes municipal arborists nervous. Seville pruned its 50 metre specimen in 2025 specifically to reduce the risk of falling branches, and Valencia's crews need aerial platforms and help from the fire service to reach the top of theirs, 41 metres in a park in Benimamet. Barcelona's grew up inside the walled grounds of a charity house in the Raval, which is the only reason there was open soil for it in the densest neighbourhood in the city.

species.name: Rubber Fig
species.intro: Most people know Ficus elastica as the thing in the corner of the living room that stops when it hits the ceiling. On Drosopoulou Street in Athens it is 26.55 metres tall, higher than the apartment blocks either side of it. Seville's began as one of those: a containerised specimen the city kept for dressing squares during celebrations, put into the ground in 1972 beside a monument to a bullfighter and left there. Fifty four years later its trunk is 5.86 metres round and its crown covers the whole of the Plaza del Altozano, the only shade on it. Lisbon's got out of a cracked pot in Mouraria and drove its roots into the street between two building fronts, and nobody can say who put the pot there or when. Three cities, three trees, and two of them were once in a pot.

species.name: Sago Palm
species.intro: A sago palm is not a palm at all. Cycas revoluta belongs to the cycads, a lineage that predates flowering plants, largely unchanged since before the dinosaurs, and it grows to match: sometimes a centimetre or two of height a year. That patience is why the three specimens mapped here, each 5.5 to 5.9 metres tall, still count as remarkable. One, beside a museum in Kagoshima, carries the name of a discovery rather than an age: in 1896 a botanist found this species' sperm cells swimming inside an ovule, the first time motile sperm had ever been seen in a seed plant. Another, a clump of roughly ninety stems at a Shizuoka temple, is one of Japan's Three Great Cycads and, by legend, close to a thousand years old. The third stands in Seville's Alcázar gardens, native to Japan, toxic throughout, rated in perfect health at its last survey.

species.name: Saw-leaf Zelkova
species.intro: A Korean queen is recorded resting under one of these in 1882, in disguise, on her way out of a capital where soldiers had just stormed the palace over unpaid wages. The zelkova at Hwayang-dong is about 700 years old and has not moved since, twenty eight metres tall with a trunk seven and a half metres round. In Japan the species is keyaki, the timber temple carpenters and taiko drum makers reach for first, which is a decent explanation for why very large ones are uncommon. Kyoto's grows just inside one of the gates of the old palace enclosure and its age is a straight blank. Florence's has been measured three times in forty years, 3.30 metres round in 1980 and 4.40 in 2021, so you can watch it grow without waiting around.

species.name: Scots Pine
species.intro: Scots pine is the plainest tree here and one of the toughest: the only pine native to nearly all of Europe, from Spain to Siberia, growing wherever the soil is too thin or sandy for anything grander. That toughness is what kept these three alive and worth the walk. Helsinki's grows on a rocky shore beside a Bronze Age burial cairn built around 2000 BC, itself around 340 years old and barely 10 metres tall, stunted by three centuries rooted in bare granite. Strasbourg's did the opposite with its lifetime: a bole the city's own register calls tortuous, twisting up into a crown flattened into a parasol, ivy climbing but never feeding on the bark. Vilnius protects its pine by name alone, a single tree on a wooded hillside above the Song Valley amphitheatre, with nothing else written down. Three cities, three ways of surviving on thin ground.

species.name: Sea Fig
species.intro: Ficus superba is a strangler fig from the edge of the subtropics, and it stops almost exactly where these three trees stand. Its range runs up from Taiwan and the Ryukyus and gives out around southern Kyushu, which is why nobody further north has heard of one and why Kagoshima alone protects four by name. The oldest sits on the side of an active volcano: the city's own signboard puts it near a thousand years, a figure three times the next-oldest tree on the register and resting on no published method, so take it as an official estimate rather than a measurement. At Nojima Shrine on the Nichinan coast, akou figs pour their roots over walls and rock through the whole precinct, and almost every visitor assumes the entire grove is protected; only one tree there actually carries the 1941 national designation. Three mapped so far, across two cities.

species.name: Sessile Oak
species.intro: Sessile oak, Quercus petraea, is the pedunculate oak's straighter-trunked cousin: its acorns sit directly on the twig with no stalk, while its leaves carry the longer stalk the other species' acorns lack. In the Netherlands it is a genuine rarity, over 95 percent of the country's oaks are pedunculate, which is what made a single tree in Groningen's Zuiderplantsoen worth a public campaign when the city nearly felled it for a footpath in 2025. Germany's royal gardens kept better company: on Pfaueninsel, the private island a Prussian king filled with peacocks and follies, sessile oaks were already a century old when the landscaping began in 1793, and three still stand there, one carrying a door cut clean through its trunk since some forgotten fit of eighteenth century theatre. These are the sessile oaks mapped on the site so far.

species.name: Silk Floss Tree
species.intro: In Spanish it is the palo borracho, the drunken stick, and the trunk is the reason: green, swollen through the middle, tapering at both ends and studded with fat conical thorns. Ceiba speciosa comes from Argentina and Brazil, stores water in that belly and flowers pink in October, when the branches are half bare and the flowers are all there is to see. The one in the small Jardim Alfredo Keil turns a whole Lisbon garden pink for a few weeks. Naples' has the widest trunk of the 53 entries the national monumental register holds for that city. Malaga's survived the remodelling of the streets around the cathedral by being built into the result. The fourth stands in the Parque Genoves in Cadiz, undated, which is normal for a tree that puts on girth this quickly.

species.name: Silky Oak
species.intro:
Grevillea robusta is not an oak, and it is not related to any tree that uses the name. It belongs to the protea family alongside banksias, native to the rainforest fringe of eastern Australia, and the site has three mapped.

Brisbane's, in the species' own homeland, is 32 metres tall and roughly a century old, taller than almost any grevillea gets. Setubal's, in Portugal, flowers in spring with dense one-sided combs of orange, more like a bottlebrush than anything most people picture when they hear silky oak. Barcelona's carries the most disputed measurements of the three: a municipal register puts its girth at 4.1 metres, an independent 2017 measurement found barely half that.

The wood was once prized by cabinetmakers for a silvery figure in the grain, which is where the common name comes from.

species.name: Silver Fir
species.intro: A silver fir this old is rare precisely because the species is not: Abies alba covers mountain slopes across central Europe by the million, so a single named, dated, individually remarkable specimen stands out against a background of forestry. The Waldhaustanne in the Bayerischer Wald is the extreme case, Germany's tallest, thickest and oldest documented silver fir, unrecorded until a family out walking reported it in 2020: about 53 metres tall, 6.93 metres round and roughly 605 years old, home to 274 recorded species and reached by a boardwalk built to keep boots off its roots. Priekulė's, by contrast, earns its fame from restraint, a single fir a Lithuanian town thought worth its own signpost at a crossroads. Aarhus's stands forty and a half metres over a private family graveyard moved wholesale into Moesgård's park in 1926. Three mapped so far, each a fir that got singled out from a forest.

species.name: Silver Lime
species.intro: Silver lime carries its identifying trick on the underside of every leaf: a coat of fine white felt that flickers the whole crown between green and silver on a windy day, readable from thirty metres away. Four trees are mapped here, and no two arrived the same way. Tilburg's oldest tree, standing off the main square where nobody thinks to look, grows in a town that may take its own name from the species. A second Tilburg lime, in a small park on the Fokkerpad, once stood in a private garden laid out by the landscape architect Leonard Springer before the estate opened to the public. Helmond's was planted just after Kasteel Helmond changed hands in 1921, the last tree of the old private park rather than a survivor of it. Amersfoort's is grafted, a weeping 'Petiolaris' crown joined onto an ordinary lime rootstock, two plants sharing one trunk, its long leaf stalks letting each leaf swivel independently in the wind.

species.name: Silver Maple
species.intro: Silver maple grows fast, splits easily in a storm, and is usually gone before it turns a hundred, which makes every old one on this list an exception to its own species. Acer saccharinum comes from the flooded river bottoms of eastern North America, where it is built to take a spring deluge that would kill less flexible trees. In Den Bosch it stands with a plane and a lime on a surviving 17th-century bastion, and separately along the old inner-city water at roughly 110 years and 25 metres. In Madrid's walled Cecilio Rodriguez garden one gave up on a single trunk early and grew four. Poznan made its finest specimen, a 105-year-old on Zakrzewski, an official natural monument. Three cities, three very different reasons the tree was allowed to keep going.

species.name: Small-leaved Lime
species.intro: For centuries in this part of Europe you were tried under one of these. The Gerichtslinde, the court lime, was a real institution: a broad tree on the village square with benches beneath it, where the local court sat in the open because everybody could then see and hear what had been decided. Small-leaved lime was usually the species chosen, since it lives long, takes heavy pruning and builds exactly that kind of wide low crown. The habit of gathering under them outlasted the courts. Carters running between Vienna and Trieste stopped under Ljubljana's Furmanska lipa to buy hay for their horses, and that tree, planted in 1626, turns 400 in 2026. Zurich has been replanting the same hilltop ever since a chronicle recorded 52 limes going in at once in 1474, and twelve limes across ten cities are mapped here.

species.name: Southern Catalpa
species.intro: Not one of these three grew straight. Breda's leans so far out over the pond in Wilhelminapark that the municipality now props its lowest limbs on columns rather than lose them. Amsterdam's turns as it rises, a slow corkscrew that the national guide to the city's monumental trees names as the reason to stop and look. Milan's has spent about 136 years twisting behind a baroque fish pond in the Giardini della Guastalla, until arborists describe its trunk as closer to sculpture than to a shade tree. The species comes from a small pocket of the southeastern United States and is far commoner in European gardens than at home. Dutch gives it two names and both are literal: trompetboom for the speckled cream flowers in July, bonenboom for the long thin pods that follow.

species.name: Southern Live Oak
species.intro: Southern live oak belongs to the humid coastal South, hung with Spanish moss and rarely far from salt air, which makes the mapped specimens here a study in the tree leaving home. One grows on a university mall in the Mojave desert, the state's largest recorded, ignoring every rule about its native range. Three stand in Dallas: two in Dealey Plaza, where the branches over Elm Street framed the shots fired at President Kennedy in 1963 and have stood over that ground ever since, and a stand of nineteen at Ferris Plaza that a mayor and a preservation coalition saved from removal in 1998 to keep a roost of grackles from being disturbed. None of these are the wild, low, shading giants of a Georgia churchyard. They are the species doing its ordinary trick, holding a canopy through drought and heat, in cities that happen to remember why it mattered.

species.name: Southern Magnolia
species.intro: For a few weeks in early summer this tree opens cream white flowers the width of a dinner plate, lemon scented and finished within a couple of days. Magnolia grandiflora comes from the warm swamp forests of the American southeast and only reached Europe in the middle of the eighteenth century, which puts a hard ceiling on how old any of these can be. The oldest here is Rome's, roughly 275 years, and it does not stand in a garden at all: it grows on the pavement of Via Corsini, outside the wall of the palace whose garden it was planted for. Padua's went in during 1786, the year Goethe came through the gate. Frederick Douglass planted two at Cedar Hill for his wife, on family testimony rather than a receipt. Thirteen mapped, in ten cities, and the leaves stay glossy and green all winter.

species.name: Spanish Fir
species.intro: The Spanish fir survives wild in only three small patches of mountain behind Ronda and Grazalema, left behind when the ice age retreated and the climate around it dried out everywhere else in Europe. Botanists did not describe Abies pinsapo until the 1830s, and within decades it was already in gardens across the continent, which is how one now stands in the royal parterres of La Granja de San Ildefonso, 700 kilometres from the nearest wild tree. The Sierra de las Nieves trees mapped here show how strange the species gets at home: Las Escaleretas has its own natural monument decree, La Perra forks into a candelabrum instead of a single spire, and the Solitary Pinsapo stands completely alone on bare rock. Four so far, three wild and one transplanted.

species.name: St Lucie Cherry
species.intro: Prunus mahaleb is usually a shrub, six metres tall on a good day, grown mostly as rootstock for other cherries rather than as a specimen in its own right. Three trees on this site ignore that description entirely. Budapest's, in the ELTE Fuveszkert botanical garden, stands 11.2 metres tall with a trunk 339 centimetres round, already growing on a nobleman's private estate before the university bought the ground around it in 1847. Den Bosch's, rooted for roughly a century against the medieval city wall on Parklaan, was nominated for the Dutch national Bomen Top 50 in 2022. Matera's, the thinnest evidenced of the three, has given its name to the city's Lanera district even though this pass could not confirm whether it still stands. Hungarians call the species sajmeggy, the Dutch call it Weichselboom; both names describe a fruit few gardeners plant a tree this size to get.

species.name: Stone Pine
species.intro: The stone pine is the tree that gives the Mediterranean skyline its flat topped silhouette, and it normally does that from a bare trunk ten or fifteen metres up, spreading wider than it grows tall. The one on Florence's Bobolino hillside ignores the rule and stands 31.5 metres. Two on a Setubal street are older than the street, left over from woodland the city expanded across, which is why they stand in no pattern at all. Istanbul's Ata Fistik Cami gave a whole hill its name and was brought there from the Aegean rather than growing there naturally. Naples has the odd one out: the pine above Mergellina was arguably the most photographed tree on earth for a century, and the tree standing on that hillside now was planted in 1995 in place of the original. Six cities so far, eight trees.

species.name: Strawberry Tree
species.intro: Madrid put one of these on its coat of arms, a bear reaching up into the branches, and the tree on the Plaza de la Lealtad is the closest thing the city has to the original. The species is normally a shrub you can see over the top of, which makes the one on Via alla Rocca in Bergamo peculiar: 16 metres tall, with a trunk 355 centimetres around. Autumn is the moment to go. Arbutus unedo flowers and ripens fruit at the same time, so a single branch carries white bells and red fruit at once, the fruit being last year's flowers finally finishing their year. Florence's grows in the Giardino dell'Iris. The fourth stands on a wine estate above Nice at the Chateau de Cremat, whose owners kept rebuilding the same hillside into grander versions of itself.

species.name: Sweet Chestnut
species.intro: In January 1949 a runaway bus above Trento was stopped by a chestnut tree, and local accounts still argue about which one. Sweet chestnut collects that kind of story because it stays around long enough: the one in Ashton Park in Bristol is about 600 years old, and the three at Arnhem, known locally as Hans, Gretel and the Witch, have been standing roughly 370. The trunk gives the age away better than any plaque, because as a chestnut ages its bark starts to spiral around the stem, and on the oldest trees the whole trunk looks wrung out like a towel. Charles II is behind the Greenwich Park tree, one of the chestnuts planted for the formal avenues he ordered cut through the park after taking the throne in 1660. Six are mapped, including the oldest tree in Edinburgh's Botanics, which was growing there before the garden arrived.

species.name: Sweet Osmanthus
species.intro: Osmanthus fragrans is grown for one thing: for a few weeks each autumn, a mature tree's small flowers put out one of the strongest scents any hardy plant makes, apricot and ripe peach carried well past the tree itself. It rarely receives official protection of its own, which is what makes two of the three trees mapped here unusual: Gunma's Kezoji and Ora's Eimeiji examples both hold National Natural Monument status normally reserved for giant conifers and camphors. Both have also outlived their own trunks. Typhoons killed the original tree at each site, and what stands today grew back from the same root or stump, still carrying the designation. Caserta's tree, in the English Garden of the royal palace, is different again: it never fell, and its 6.5-metre girth is several stems bundled together rather than one trunk, which is how the species actually grows.

species.name: Sycamore
species.intro: Nobody plants a sycamore on purpose any more. It seeds itself into gutters, railway banks and any gap it can find across northern Europe, grows fast, and gets cut down long before it becomes anything, which is precisely what makes an old one worth looking up at. Glasgow's Darnley Sycamore is put at 450 to 500 years, exceptional for a species that rarely passes 400, and it carries the name of Mary, Queen of Scots' husband on a story from 1565. Copenhagen's is the thickest tree inside Assistens cemetery and the least exotic species in it. Edinburgh's grows sideways out of solid rock at the start of a riverside walkway, with no recorded age and no need of one. Eight are mapped, one in each of eight cities, from Reykjavik down to Barcelona, where the summers are hot enough that the species barely holds on.

species.name: Tasmanian Blue Gum
species.intro: A trunk 5.2 metres around on a tree planted in 1904 is what a blue gum does when nothing gets in its way. Eucalyptus globulus comes from Tasmania and southeastern Australia and puts on size faster than almost anything else that grows this big, which is why nineteenth century Europe planted it everywhere: for timber, for drying out marshland, and on the belief that its oils cleaned bad air. The tree on the hotel road at Bucaco is 7.15 metres around at about 150 years old, thicker than anything else on that walk. Naples' reaches 30 metres, the tallest tree the registers record inside the botanical garden. Madrid's stands north of the Estanque in the Retiro and is over a century old. Four are mapped, and every one of them is younger than it looks.

species.name: Tipu Tree
species.intro: None of the Lisbon tipus stands anywhere a gardener would have chosen. One holds down a traffic circle, where a crown 34 metres across had become the city's problem by 2018. One stands in the middle of a bus terminal. One occupies the triangle of grass outside parliament, which has kept a South American tree on its doorstep for about ninety years. The fourth grows in the garden named for the Portuguese defeat at La Lys in 1918. Tipuana tipu comes from the foothills of Bolivia and Argentina, a legume with feathery leaves and single winged pods that spin down like sycamore keys, and it puts up with pavement, drought and hard pruning better than most things. The Barcelona tree, about 101 years old, is the specimen the city measures its other tipus against, and there are plenty to measure: it is one of the commonest street trees in the city.

species.name: Tree of Heaven
species.intro: Ailanthus altissima is the tree cities spend the most money getting rid of, and all four of these are protected or plaqued instead. The one in Ravenscourt Park in London has a green plaque at its foot. Zaragoza lists the specimen in its botanical garden as a singular tree. Dublin's is the largest in Ireland, framed between two Victorian glasshouses, and its age is a real argument: the register says 120 to 165 years, the way this species grows suggests closer to 70 or 100. That growth rate is the whole problem with it. Tree of heaven seeds into any crack, sends suckers under pavement and shades out whatever stood there first, fast enough to reach a serious size within one lifetime. The Danish name says what that looks like: skyraekker, sky reacher. Copenhagen's, in Assistens, is 15.5 metres.

species.name: Tulip Tree
species.intro: You can identify it from the pavement: the leaf looks as though someone snipped the tip off with scissors, four lobes and a flat end where the point should be. The oldest here exists because of the post. On 1 October 1716 a London apothecary sent seed of a barely known American tree to Leiden, and eleven days later Herman Boerhaave sowed it in the botanical garden where it still stands, now about 310 years old. Everything else on this page was planted too, with one exception: the Queens Giant in New York came up on its own in a stretch of forest that was never cleared, is dated to at least 368 years and is the tallest carefully measured tree in the city. Porto holds four of the eleven, including one whose crown is wider than the tree is tall.

species.name: Turkey Oak
species.intro: Quercus cerris is native to southeastern Europe and Asia Minor, and every planting mapped here happened on purpose: gardeners liked how fast it grows and how large it gets while the person who planted it is still around to see it. Genoa's, in the English-style grounds of Villa Serra above the city, is the surprise: 41 metres, taller than the Californian redwood sixty metres away, a height this oak rarely reaches in its own range. Caserta's grows in the royal park's English Garden among trees collected from Australia and California, thirty-five metres and about 150 years old. Utrecht's four stand together on an old city-wall bastion, close enough that the Dutch register counts them as one entry rather than four, two planted around 1835 and two around 1870. The leaves give it away: stiffer and more deeply cut than a pedunculate oak's, with whiskery bud scales and mossy, curl-wrapped acorn cups.

species.name: Turkish Hazel
species.intro: A hazel is supposed to be a shrub you can see over. The Turkish hazel puts up a single straight trunk instead and keeps going: the one in the Square du Temple in Paris stands sixteen metres tall with a trunk 235 centimetres around. The Amsterdam tree, planted in the Hortus in 1795, is called the oldest and thickest of its kind in the Netherlands by the Dutch tree foundation. Romania has only two officially protected specimens of Corylus colurna and one of them grows in Cismigiu in Bucharest. Vienna protected a pair in the Resselpark in 1972 for the way they match, though they went in seventeen years apart, in 1900 and 1917. The best line about any of them belongs to French regional television, which ran a news piece written in the voice of the hazel in Square Maurice-Gardette: I am 145, stop cracking my hazelnuts.

species.name: Turkish Pine
species.intro: Pinus brutia goes by three different names depending on where you stand in front of it: Turkish pine in English, pino bruzio or pin de Calabre on the ground in Italy and France, pino de Creta in Spain, describing a pine from Turkey, Cyprus, Crete and the Levant that colonises burnt ground first and produces a honey beekeepers actively seek. Botanists still argue whether it deserves its own species or belongs folded into the Aleppo pine; the national register in Florence files its specimen under Pinus halepensis regardless. Three cities map one each, and each shows a different way an old pine stands: Florence's has grown a lopsided, storm-prone flag crown after a century squeezed into a crowded botanical collection, Rouen's needed a support structure built under it in 2021, and Valencia's went straight up for thirty metres without leaning, forking or flattening at all.

species.name: Turner's Oak
species.intro: Turner's oak is a garden invention, not a wild species: an English nursery crossed the evergreen Mediterranean holm oak with the northern pedunculate oak in the late eighteenth century, and the hybrid kept the holm oak's leathery leaves through winter, only dropping them in spring when new growth pushes the old ones off. Three specimens are mapped here. Amsterdam's, in the Hortus Botanicus, still carries its graft union thirty centimetres above the ground and a disputed planting year, 1865 by the city's own register or 1895 by the Bomenstichting's, thirty years apart on the same tree. Brussels has two, a few minutes' walk apart on the same lawns of Parc d'Egmont: the one entered into the region's tree register in 1999, and a taller, thicker neighbour registered separately nearby. None of the three is old by oak standards. All three are odd enough to be worth the detour.

species.name: Weeping Beech
species.intro: A weeping beech makes a room. The branches drop from the top of the trunk to the ground in a closed curtain, and the space inside is dark, hollow and tall enough to stand up in, which is most of the reason cities hold on to them. Munich's ordinance is unusually frank about that: the reason recorded for protecting the beech by the Schwanenbrucke is that people are fond of it. The same city protects a second one on Situlistrasse on the grounds that it is the largest weeping beech standing in Munich, and says so in its own paperwork. The Leiden tree, about 185 years old in the Hortus, has the longest paper trail, running back to the London nurseryman George Loddiges. Copenhagen's grows in Assistens, the cemetery the city treats as a park.

species.name: Weeping Fig
species.intro: The genuinely large, old weeping figs people go to see split into two very different stories. In Miriam Vale, Queensland, on the coast road to Agnes Water, one fig has grown to roughly 12 metres round and 35 metres across, doing duty since around the 1890s as the town's milk depot, its war memorial shelter and an impromptu vet's surgery, all under one crown. Brisbane's stands at the Alice Street gate of the City Botanic Gardens, about 155 years old, planted not long after the gardens themselves were founded, native ground for a species that grows wild across northern Australia and South and Southeast Asia. Lisbon's is the odd one out, five metres round in the Campo de Santana park, doing the same unlikely, enormous work eight thousand kilometres from where the species grows on its own. All three keep their leaves year-round and none has ever stopped spreading wider rather than taller, which is the whole trick of the tree.

species.name: Weeping Higan Cherry
species.intro: Half of these are stand-ins for a more famous tree, and in Kyoto nobody minds. The weeping cherry everyone photographs at Maruyama Park is the second one on the spot, the original having gone. The Taiko cherry at Daigo-ji is not the tree Toyotomi Hideyoshi saw when he staged his enormous blossom party there in the spring of 1598, months before his death, but it stands where the party happened. Shidarezakura hang their flowering branches straight down, so the tree makes a curtain you walk under rather than a canopy you look up into, and they open before the ordinary somei-yoshino. Nara's is the extreme case: the weeping cherry beside the approach to Himuro Shrine opens before any other cherry in the city, and the local spring is dated from it. The fourth came out of the Kyoto Imperial Palace grounds as a gift, in the reign of Emperor Komei.

species.name: Weeping Willow
species.intro: The weeping willow is not built to last. It is fast-growing and soft-wooded, the sort of tree that usually falls to storm or age long before it earns a place beside the oaks and yews this site otherwise maps. That makes its exceptions worth naming. In Hiroshima, one stood 370 metres from the point the atomic bomb detonated in 1945 and is still alive today, the closest registered survivor the city has. In Leiden, one has wept over the statue of Pieter van der Werf for more than a century, its own history otherwise unrecorded by any source found so far. In Alkmaar, a third bends over an 1876 victory monument in a park laid out by the Zocher family, who also reshaped the city's old bastions. None of these three are ancient by this site's usual standards. They earn their place by surviving what a short-lived species rarely manages.

species.name: Western Red Cedar
species.intro: Two of the three cedars on this page are slowly walking away from where they were planted. Western red cedar layers: its lowest branches bend under their own weight, touch the ground, root where they land and thicken into trunks of their own. Do that for a century and a half and one tree becomes a small colony walking somewhere. Sintra's has been heading toward the lake below Pena Palace for about that long, and forestry students have used it as a teaching example since at least 1916. Strasbourg's is doing the same thing in the Parc de l'Orangerie, which is rare to see in a public park, because ground level branches are usually the first thing a maintenance crew removes. Cork's takes a different shape entirely: limbs running out sideways, each thicker than most full grown trees, and a low fence around it because everyone's first instinct is to climb.

species.name: White Mulberry
species.intro: These trees were planted as machinery. White mulberry leaf is the only thing a silkworm will eat, so every ruler who fancied a silk industry ordered mulberries into the ground, and the trees stayed long after the venture folded. Christian IV tried it in Denmark, and the mulberry at Proviantgarden is the one tree from that royal scheme anyone can still point to. Maria Theresa's push put orchards across Taban in Buda, which is most likely where Budapest's oldest mulberry comes from, whatever the Ottoman legend says. Around Bergamo the leaves fed trays of larvae in farmhouse lofts, and three of those trees still stand in a public garden. Split's, in the courtyard of Hajduk's first ground, was DNA sampled in 2015 and cloned 105 times, once per year of the club. Nine cities so far, and every tree on this page is a leftover from an industry that failed.

species.name: White Oak
species.intro: White oak is eastern North America's slow, wide-crowned oak, tougher and longer-lived than red oak, and the three we map range from a fundraiser to a courtroom curiosity. The oldest, on the edge of Old Logan Cemetery in Ohio, is put at roughly six hundred years; the town sells its acorns as saplings to keep the line going. Boston's grows wild on the Arnold Arboretum's Peters Hill turf, uncatalogued until 2010 and cored in 2018 to roughly two centuries old, possibly the oldest tree in the whole collection. Athens, Georgia's is younger and stranger: an eighty-year-old planted in 1946 from the acorn of a white oak an 1890 newspaper story said legally owned itself, a claim courts have never accepted and the city has never stopped repeating.

species.name: White Poplar
species.intro: White poplars rarely get the chance to grow old. The species spreads fast by root suckers and gets cleared as a nuisance long before it reaches any real size, which is part of why the three mapped here stand out. Lithuania's Vainiai Poplar is the giant of the three, 6.85 metres round and among the largest of its kind recorded in the country, still standing in a former manor park that has otherwise reverted to scrub. Warsaw's example, in a small Rakowiec neighbourhood park, was made a natural monument in 1987 and shares its corner with two other protected trees. Amsterdam's is the odd one out: its own protection register admits it is no longer an impressive specimen and keeps it listed anyway, on the strength of being, most likely, the oldest living thing in its park. Three very different reasons to notice the same overlooked species.

species.name: White Willow
species.intro: White willow is a river tree that rarely gets old. It roots fast on a gravel bar scoured clean by a flood, grows up in crowded thickets, and by forty or fifty years is usually splitting apart under its own soft, fast-grown wood. The ones that reach two centuries are almost always the ones that were pollarded, cut back hard to the same point on the trunk every few years, which is the history behind Alkmaar's willow in the old Veenbos polder, closing in on two hundred years old. Munich's stands alone on the Isar's northern floodplain, unusual enough on its own that the city's 2021 natural monument ordinance protects it for that solitude. Gdansk's, beside a pond in Oliwa, survived an arson attack on 29 December 2025 that burned out its core before firefighters arrived in time to save the second protected willow growing next to it.

species.name: Wild Olive
species.intro: A wild olive hollows out as it ages, which is what makes every age on this page an estimate rather than a measurement: no ring count survives in a trunk that has lost its heartwood. All three grow in Sardinia, in the granite hills of Gallura and the coast of Ogliastra, and together they are the closest thing Italy has to an age record. S'Ozzastru, at Santu Baltolu di Carana near Luras, is Italy's oldest living tree by most estimates: the University of Sassari puts it at 2,500 to 4,000 years, its trunk 11.5 metres round, and Sardinians call it su babbu mannu, the great father. A second, unnamed olivastro grows a few metres along the same path, half the girth at 5.4 metres and overshadowed by its neighbour, though nowhere else on the island would it go unnoticed. The third stands alone in the village square of Santa Maria Navarrese, beside a church five centuries its junior, its trunk scarred by an arson attempt in the early 1960s that it survived. All three were declared natural monuments by the region, in 1991 and 1994, and all three are free to visit.

species.name: Willowleaf Podocarp
species.intro: Three of these stand on this site, two in Rome and one in Singapore, and each is protected for a different reason. Podocarps are a mostly southern conifer family that split off before pines existed and never adopted the cone: the seed sits instead on a swollen, fleshy stalk that turns purple and gets eaten by birds, which is how the species spread from the Himalayan foothills to New Guinea and why Buddhist communities planted it around temples across that range. Rome's Villa Sciarra specimen made Italy's national monumental register for a single reason, botanical rarity, with no claim to age or size at all; the city calls it splendid and enormous anyway. A second Rome tree, in Piazza Vittorio's garden, is one of the largest in the city and was listed in 2025. Singapore's grows on a lawn in the Botanic Gardens, its own age never recorded.

species.name: Wych Elm
species.intro: On the night of 12 May 1971 a crowd of Stockholmers climbed into the elms of Kungstradgarden and refused to come down, and the city workers went home. Those trees are still standing, between 160 and 205 years old. Any wych elm of size is worth a detour in western Europe now, because a fungus carried tree to tree by bark beetles cleared out most of the big ones within two generations. That absence is why the other four are here at all. Munich protects the elm on Maximiliansplatz precisely because almost every elm that size in the city has gone, and Trinity College Dublin, which once counted around sixty across its grounds, is down to one worth naming. Trento's stands in the garden facing the station, under two minutes from the platform. The Toulouse tree is simply a big elm, which for this species is the entire story.

species.name: Wych Elm 'Exoniensis'
species.intro: This is the feather elm, pluimiep in Dutch, a cultivar of wych elm bred narrow and upright where the wild species spreads wide, and grafted about 1.5 metres up the trunk to keep that shape. Old wych elms of any kind are a rare sight after a century of Dutch elm disease took most of them out, which is reason enough to go looking for the three this site maps, all of them, by coincidence of where the registers have looked, standing in Leeuwarden. Two grow in the small Vosseparkje at the edge of the old town, a short walk apart and told apart mainly by which one stands nearer the pond. The third is a street planting on Molenstraat, where the graft union on the larger of the pair has swollen into a scar tissue collar over five metres round, wider at that one point than the trunk beneath it, with a fern rooted in its canopy. None of the three has a written history beyond the national monument register. What they have is a shape nobody plants any more and a graft nobody has fully explained.
